text: Classes Arx class declarations use annotation lines for modifiers. Declaration lines stay minimal: a field starts with its name, and a method starts with fn . Class Syntax class Counter(BaseCounter, Audited): @[public, static, constant] version: int32 = 1 value: int32 = 0 @[private] internal: int32 = 1 fn get(self) -> int32: return self.value @[protected] fn process(self, x: int32) -> int32: return x + 1 Optional class-level annotations use the same surface form: @[public, abstract] class Shape: @[public, abstract] fn area(self) -> float64 Template methods use the same @<...> prefix form as module functions. Method modifiers and template parameters may appear in either order as long as each prefix stays on its own line above the method declaration: class Math: @<T: i32 | f64> @[public, static] fn identity(value: T) -> T: return value Annotation Rules Modifiers must be written as @[...] on the line immediately above the target declaration. Modifiers never appear before the declaration name or before fn . Annotation lists are comma-separated and must not be empty. An annotation must be followed by exactly one declaration. Floating annotations are rejected. Supported modifiers: Visibility: public , private , protected Storage and mutability: static , constant , mutable Declaration metadata: abstract , extern Not supported yet: override , virtual , final , sealed , readonly , inline Defaults Defaults are applied during parsing and normalization, not written back as implicit annotation lines. Fields default to public visibility and mutable mutability. Methods default to public visibility. Only explicitly written modifiers are preserved as explicit metadata on the emitted IRx/ASTx nodes. For example, these declarations are equivalent semantically: value: int32 = 0 fn get(self) -> int32: return self.value @[public, mutable] value: int32 = 0 @[public] fn get(self) -> int32: return self.value Construction And Typed Class Values Declared classes can be used in type annotations and construction expressions. Counter() remains valid when no required initializer parameters are declared. An optional __init__ hook adds positional arguments, constructor keywords, and literal defaults; an optional __del__ hook runs at final release. class Counter: @[public, static, constant] version: int32 = 3 fn get(self) -> int32: return 1 class CounterFactory: @[public, static] fn make() -> Counter: return Counter() fn take_counter(counter: Counter) -> int32: return counter.get() fn main() -> int32: var counter: Counter = CounterFactory.make() return take_counter(counter) + Counter.version This surface syntax maps directly onto IRx-owned class nodes: Counter in annotations becomes astx.ClassType Counter(...) becomes astx.ClassConstruct with ordered arguments/keywords Counter.version becomes astx.StaticFieldAccess CounterFactory.make() becomes astx.StaticMethodCall Lifecycle Hooks class Counter: value: i32 = 0 fn __init__(self, value: i32 = 1) -> none: self.value = value return none fn __del__(self) -> none: print(self.value) return none fn main() -> i32: var counter: Counter = Counter(value=7) var alias: Counter = counter counter = Counter(3) assert alias.value == 7 return 0 The two variables initially refer to the same object; copying a reference does not copy fields. Reassignment releases only the replaced reference. Locals, discarded temporaries, loop-body locals, and early returns release their references on ordinary lexical exits. Final release calls __del__ exactly once, then drops owned fields and frees storage. Returns preserve object identity and can outlive the creating function. Calls borrow objects; evaluated class arguments and receivers are pinned before later arguments can replace fields. Rebinding a class parameter replaces its independent local reference, not the caller's binding. Hook rules: Double-underscore (dunder) method names are reserved for language protocols. The supported lifecycle names are __init__ and __del__ ; unknown names such as __inti__ or __str__ are semantic errors, including on static methods. Lifecycle hooks cannot be declared as fields. Plain init and deinit are ordinary method names, not compatibility aliases. Existing IRx __enter__ and __exit__ context protocols remain recognized and callable, but do not enable Arx with syntax. Dunders identify language-defined behavior, not private visibility or inheritance from a universal builtin superclass. Implementations are written by users; normal visibility annotations still apply. __init__(self, ...) -> none and __del__(self) -> none are compiler entry points, not ordinary callable methods. Explicit calls are rejected. Hooks cannot be static, abstract, external, overloaded, templated, or variadic. Constructor defaults are existing scalar/string literals, not resource values. Constructor arguments bind by parameter name, excluding self . Unknown, duplicate, missing, excessive, and incompatible arguments are errors. Supplied expressions evaluate once in source order, including keywords. A class without its own __init__ has a zero-argument constructor. Base hooks run with their defaults; a base requiring arguments is rejected when constructing the derived class. Explicit base-argument forwarding is deferred. Shared ancestors initialize once in canonical base-first storage order. Each phase initializes its declared fields before calling its own __init__ . Final release reverses those phases, calling each __del__ before dropping its fields in reverse declaration order. This also works through a base-typed reference; non-prefix multiple-inheritance views locate concrete storage. Inside hooks, self is only a field-access receiver: it cannot be aliased, returned, passed elsewhere, or used to invoke an ordinary self method. This prevents escape during construction and resurrection during destruction. These names are familiar from Python, but Arx keeps its own lifecycle contract: normal final-reference release synchronously runs cleanup, base phases chain automatically, and direct hook calls and resurrection are forbidden. This does not add Python's garbage collector, super() chaining, __new__ , or unwinding after fatal errors. Ordinary operations such as close() remain callable and are separate from object destruction. Ordinary instance and static methods also accept named arguments. An instance receiver is implicit; it cannot be supplied as a keyword. Keywords bind against the statically selected declaration, including through inheritance and dynamic dispatch. Values evaluate in source order, then omitted defaults in declaration order. See Functions . Direct lifecycle-hook calls remain forbidden. Owned Fields And Boundaries Scalar fields keep their existing behavior. Instance strings own independent heap copies (or move fresh owned results); replacing a string field safely releases its previous allocation. String-field reads produce owned snapshots, so evaluated arguments, local copies, and returns survive later replacement of that field. Acyclic class-reference fields hold strong references and default to empty; dereferencing an empty class value reports a checked runtime error rather than using a null pointer. Field declarations may refer to already initialized fields through self . A public File (or lowercase file ) field holds an ordinary class reference. It may be initialized with File(...) , open(...) , or another File reference, and may be replaced or shared. Empty fields use the normal checked class reference behavior. The builtin File class itself owns one private native handle initialized once by its compiler-provided constructor; users cannot extract or replace that handle. Final File release invokes normal owned-field cleanup. See the owned-file example and file API . File subclassing and reopening are deferred. This reference-counted subset is synchronous and non-atomic. Cyclic field-type graphs are rejected conservatively, including edges through assignable subtypes, even if a particular program would not create a cycle. Class values in containers/unions/struct fields, owned globals/statics, generator capture, list/Arrow/resource aggregate fields, and an external class ownership ABI are not supported. There is no garbage collector, weak reference, resurrection, explicit deletion, or thread-safe reference counting. Allocation and empty-reference failures use ARX-RUNTIME-CLASS-001 . Checked compiler-local construction failures release initialized fields, run only completed base-phase destructors, and free partial storage. Native field-release errors preserve the first error while continuing remaining field releases and freeing the object. Generated calls propagate exceptions through those cleanup edges; an implicit destructor failure preserves an existing primary exception. Unrecoverable native failures do not promise cleanup. See the exception boundary . IRx Alignment Arx now emits IRx/ASTx nodes directly instead of maintaining a separate Arx class AST layer. This is a hard repository boundary: new AST node types or new lowering behavior for class features belong in IRx/ASTx, not in Arx. class declarations lower into astx.ClassDefStmt . Base classes become astx.ClassType entries. Fields become astx.VariableDeclaration with visibility and mutability set directly, plus is_static when present. Methods become astx.FunctionDef plus astx.FunctionPrototype , with visibility set directly and is_static , is_abstract , or is_extern attached to the prototype when written. Instance member syntax like self.value lowers into astx.FieldAccess . This keeps Arx syntax aligned with the IRx semantic boundary while preserving explicit modifier intent on the same nodes that later lowering consumes. A runtime-schema dataframe[...] method parameter also accepts a statically typed DataFrame, without converting its data. An exact static-schema overload wins if present. This permits CSVStream.write(frame) and ParquetStream.write(frame) for both kinds of frame; it does not permit implicit narrowing or general numeric conversion-ranked overloads.

Instance member syntax like self.value lowers into astx.FieldAccess . This keeps Arx syntax aligned with the IRx semantic boundary while preserving explicit modifier intent on the same nodes that later lowering consumes. A runtime-schema dataframe[...] method parameter also accepts a statically typed DataFrame, without converting its data. An exact static-schema overload wins if present. This permits CSVStream.write(frame) and ParquetStream.write(frame) for both kinds of frame; it does not permit implicit narrowing or general numeric conversion-ranked overloads.
title: Classes · IRx Alignment

text: Collections and Apache Arrow Arx exposes four built-in collection families with deliberately different semantics: Surface type Purpose Runtime representation list[T] General ordered values and builtin range results IRx dynamic-list runtime tensor[T, ...] Homogeneous N-dimensional numeric data Apache Arrow C++ arrow::Tensor dataframe[...] Heterogeneous named columns Apache Arrow C++ arrow::Table series[T] One typed DataFrame column Apache Arrow C++ arrow::ChunkedArray list is not an Arrow container. Tensor, DataFrame, and Series storage is provided by IRx's native Arrow C++ runtime. Lists fn sum_values() -> i32: var values: list[i32] = range(0, 4) var total: i32 = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return total Dynamic lists are move-only: owned locals and non-transferred temporaries are released on normal and exceptional lexical exits and replacement; returning an owned list moves it to the caller. A list moved into a pending return cannot be read or reassigned through that binding in finally ; a separate fresh owned return value is allowed. Parameters borrow storage and cannot append or return that borrow. Literal-list views are non-owning and cannot escape into dynamic owners or call arguments. See the enforced list contract for the ownership boundary. range currently materializes a list, not a lazy iterator. Tensors Fixed-shape tensors use one or more integer dimensions: fn pick(grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2]) -> i32: return grid[1, 0] fn main() -> i32: var grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] return pick(grid) Rules: supported elements: i8 , i16 , i32 , i64 , f32 , and f64 literals must be rectangular and match the declared shape indexing supplies one index per static dimension variables, fields, and returns require at least one static dimension Tensor storage is readonly in the current implementation tensor[T, ...] accepts runtime shape/stride metadata at a function or extern parameter boundary: fn accept(values: tensor[i32, ...]) -> none: return none Passing the value through is supported. Dynamic indexing is not yet available, so indexed access requires a static-shape annotation. DataFrames and Series fn main() -> i32: var rows: dataframe[id: i32, score: f64] = dataframe({ id: [1, 2, 3], score: [0.5, 0.8, 1.0], }) var scores: series[f64] = rows.score var ids: series[i32] = rows["id"] print(rows.ncols()) return cast(rows.nrows(), i32) Rules: columns support signed/unsigned numeric, Boolean and string values nullable columns use T | none ; date/time/timestamp columns can be populated through literal constructors or checked RecordBatch conversions the constructor accepts list-literal columns with equal row counts; it does not add implicit signed-to-unsigned coercion names and types must match the declared static schema statically known columns use rows.name or rows["name"] nrows() and ncols() return i64 dataframe[...] supports runtime-schema locals, parameters and returns, preserving rich Arrow types/metadata through RecordBatch casts; its columns cannot be accessed statically by name or silently narrowed Use read_csv / write_csv from stdlib.csv and read_parquet / write_parquet from stdlib.parquet for file I/O. Reads return independently owned runtime-schema frames; writes borrow frames and check finalization. No format-specific DataFrame methods or to_* aliases are added. CSVStream and ParquetStream in those modules support explicit streaming via frame() and write(frame) . Schema , BatchBuilder , RecordBatch and IPC remain in stdlib.arrow . File workflows and format-specific safety limits live in CSV and Parquet ; exact casts follow the shared conversion contract below. IPCReader.next() advances one batch; batch() and schema() return independent snapshots. open_file selects IPC file format, open_stream selects streaming format at a path, and connect exchanges IPC streaming bytes over TCP. Writers reject schema mismatches, including metadata and nullability. Check is_null before typed getters. Objects close on their last scoped reference; explicit close() is idempotent. See the interoperability workflow and ownership contract . Checked DataFrame conversion cast(frame, dataframe[id:i64]) and cast(batch, dataframe[id:i64]) assert exact names, order, physical types, and every chunk's reachable nullability. They do not project, coerce, fill nulls, or infer compile-time types. Metadata and independent ownership are preserved; cast(frame, RecordBatch) bridges back to batch APIs. Runtime-schema frames preserve rich Arrow data without permitting unchecked static column access. Fixed-row-count casts, owned globals, generator locals, aggregate-owned fields, and arbitrary DataFrame FFI are unsupported. See parameterized schemas for nested nullability and exact physical parameters. File-format restrictions still apply independently of what an in-memory frame can hold. Runtime boundary IRx activates native Arrow features only when lowering requires them. Generated LLVM calls opaque C ABI functions; Arrow C++ object layouts and ownership do not leak into LLVM structs or Arx syntax. See Native Apache Arrow Support for arrays, Arrow C Data, RecordBatch IPC, and current interoperability details. Nullable scalars and Series expressions nullable[T] stores a fixed-width numeric or Boolean scalar plus a validity bit. A nullable column is spelled series[T | none] . Indexing a nullable column returns nullable[T] ; indexing a non-nullable column returns T . Indices are zero-based; negative or out-of-range indices fail at runtime. ``` title: Nullable column expressions ``` fn main() -> i32: var frame: dataframe[x:i32 | none] = dataframe({x:[1, none, 3]}) var doubled: series[i32 | none] = frame.x + frame.x var missing: nullable[i32] = doubled[1] assert is_null(missing) assert fill_null(doubled[2], 0) == 6 var filled: series[i32] = fill_null(doubled, 7) assert filled[1] == 7 var empty: nullable[i32] = none assert is_null(empty) return 0 Supported operators are + , - , * , / , == , != , < , <= , > and >= . Numeric operands use IRx common-type promotion. Column casts are checked; values that cannot be represented by the promoted type fail explicitly. Series/scalar operations broadcast the scalar. Series/Series operations require equal lengths. Integer arithmetic is checked: overflow and division by zero fail instead of wrapping. Null operands produce null outputs, including comparisons. Boolean && / and and || / or propagate nulls strictly, not with Kleene semantics. These operations are eager, not short-circuiting. is_null returns bool for a nullable scalar or a non-nullable Boolean Series mask. fill_null(value, replacement) eagerly evaluates a matching non-null scalar replacement and returns a non-nullable scalar or Series. Nullable scalars cannot implicitly become non-nullable values or conditions. Nullable scalar globals support numeric/Boolean literal or none initializers. Direct none is accepted in nullable declarations, assignments, returns, and function arguments/defaults. It never implicitly fills a non-nullable value. These scalar operations currently cover i8 – i64 , u8 – u64 , f32 , f64 and bool . String, temporal, decimal and nested Series retain their data and schema but cannot yet be indexed into language scalars or used in these operators. Unary + and checked - support signed numeric values; Boolean ! / not invert validity-preserving masks. Unsigned negation requires an explicit cast. column[start:stop:step] follows Python's bound clipping and negative-stride rules; omitted bounds are allowed and a zero step fails. Slicing, is_null and series_count also work on rich column storage. series_sum , series_min , series_max , series_mean , series_any and series_all skip nulls and return nullable scalars: empty/all-null input has a null result. series_count returns the non-null count as i64 . Integer sums use checked i64 / u64 accumulators; floating sums and means return f64 . Boolean reductions require Boolean columns. column[index] = value updates a mutable numeric/Boolean Series binding with bounds, type and nullability checks. Aliases of that handle observe updates; the originating DataFrame and previously computed/sliced Series do not. Construction completes before publication, so failed updates leave the old column intact. Concurrent access to a mutated handle is unsupported. Updates are statements, not value-producing assignment expressions. Returned Series own independent references; temporary columns and aliases are released by normal scope-lifetime cleanup. Parameterized static DataFrame schemas Checked RecordBatch casts additionally accept: decimal128[precision, scale] and decimal256[precision, scale] . timestamp["unit"] , timestamp["unit", "timezone"] , and time["unit"] , with units s , ms , us or ns . binary , binary[positive_size] , large_binary , and large_string . arrow_list[T] , large_list[T] , and fixed_list[T, positive_size] . dictionary[index_type, value_type] (unordered). arrow_map[key_type, value_type] and arrow_struct[name:T, ...] . For example, dataframe[amount:decimal128[12, 3] | none, items:arrow_list[nullable[i32]] | none] declares nullable decimal and list columns. Nested children are non-nullable unless wrapped in nullable[T] ; this wrapper models child nullability even for types that cannot be language scalars. Map keys cannot be nullable. Rich schemas work in aliases, parameters, returns and checked RecordBatch casts. Casts check names, order, exact physical parameters and nested nullability; non-nullable top-level columns also check actual batch null counts. They do not rescale decimals, change time units, or decode dictionaries implicitly. Input schema and field metadata are preserved. Unparameterized time uses time64 microseconds; timestamp / datetime use timezone-naive timestamp microseconds. Their text literal constructors accept whole seconds without timezone or fractional components. Use parameterized storage or checked Arrow imports for other units or zones. Rich DataFrame literals use the declared schema rather than inference. Decimal cells use exact strings or integers (not binary floats); binary cells use UTF-8 strings, with fixed widths checked in bytes. Parameterized temporal cells use integer storage units, without timezone conversion. Lists use nested lists; structs use positional lists matching declared field order; maps use lists of [key, value] pairs. Dictionaries encode literal values with checked index capacity. Nested nullability, widths, precision, scale and shape are validated during semantic analysis. Lowering embeds validated Arrow IPC bytes, not a Python interpreter or handwritten serialization format. Standalone rich scalar variables remain unsupported.

text: Arx Compiler CLI The arxlang distribution installs the arx command. It can inspect frontend and lowering stages, compile native artifacts, run executables, and execute compiled tests. Command forms arx [input_file] [options] arx run [input_file] [options] arx test [paths ...] [options] run is an alternate spelling of --run . test is a separate subcommand. Inspection modes arx --show-tokens program.x arx --show-ast program.x arx --show-llvm-ir program.x These modes stop after printing the requested representation. Build and run arx program.x --output-file program arx --run program.x arx run program.x The compiler emits an executable when the module defines main . Without a native entry point, or with --lib , it emits an object artifact instead. Use arx --help for the complete option list and defaults rather than a copied flag catalog. Diagnostics and linker choices below have operational consequences. Compiling multiple input files in one invocation is not currently supported. Use project-aware imports to compile a module graph from one entry file. Output path --output-file accepts the requested artifact path. If it is omitted, the compiler derives a name from the entry source file and otherwise falls back to a.out . Link modes The default auto mode uses the platform toolchain's default executable mode. pie and no-pie request explicit position-independent or non-PIE linking. If a linker defaults to PIE but rejects an object relocation, use: arx program.x --link-mode no-pie IRx emits PIC-compatible objects by default. Explicit link modes are primarily toolchain compatibility controls. Diagnostics Expected lexer, parser, semantic, lowering, native compilation, and linking failures exit with status 1. Human-readable diagnostics go to standard error by default. Unexpected internal failures produce ARX-INTERNAL-001 without exposing exception details and exit with status 70. Compiler developers can opt in to the original Python exception and traceback with --traceback . Use --diagnostic-format json for one versioned JSON document on standard error: { "diagnostics": [ { "code": "ARX-PARSE-001", "column": 7, "end_column": null, "end_line": null, "hint": null, "line": 4, "message": "expected expression", "module": null, "notes": [], "phase": "frontend", "severity": "error" } ], "schema_version": 1 } JSON mode covers expected compiler-phase failures and sanitized internal failures. Argument usage errors remain argparse text with exit status 2. Consumers must reject unsupported schema_version values instead of guessing field semantics. Exit status Meaning 0 command succeeded 1 expected compiler/source failure 2 CLI usage or input-path failure 70 unexpected internal compiler failure Tests The arx test subcommand has its own discovery and execution options. See Compiled Tests . API boundary CLI argument handling lives in Arx. Semantic diagnostics, LLVM lowering, artifact building, and runtime feature activation are provided by IRx.

text: Control Flow Arx currently supports if / else , while , and two for loop styles. If / Else ``` title: If/else example summary: Branches based on a comparison. ``` fn abs_value(x: i32) -> i32: ``` title: abs_value summary: Returns absolute value of x. ``` if x < 0: return 0 - x else: return x While Loop ``` title: While loop example summary: Repeats while condition is true. ``` fn count_to_ten() -> i32: ``` title: count_to_ten summary: Increments value until it reaches ten. ``` var a: i32 = 0 while a < 10: a = a + 1 return a For Loop (For-In Style) For-in loops iterate over list-valued expressions, including builtin range(start, stop[, step]) , list literals, and list variables: for i in <list-expression>: ``` title: Range-style for loop summary: Iterates from start to end with the builtin range helper. ``` fn range_loop(n: i32) -> i32: ``` title: range_loop summary: Sums values produced by a range loop. ``` var total: i32 = 0 for i in range(0, n): total = total + i return total You can also iterate over a list literal or a list variable: ``` title: List for-in loop summary: Iterates over one list variable and one list literal. ``` fn list_loop() -> i32: ``` title: list_loop summary: Sums values from two list-valued loop inputs. ``` var values: list[i32] = range(0, 3) var total: i32 = 0 for value in values: total = total + value for value in [3, 4]: total = total + value return total The old colon range header syntax was removed. Use builtin range(...) or any other list-valued expression instead. For Loop (Count Style) Count-style loops follow: for var i: type = init; condition; update: ``` title: Count-style for loop summary: Uses initializer, condition, and update expressions. ``` fn count_loop() -> i32: ``` title: count_loop summary: Sums numbers from 0 to 4. ``` var total: i32 = 0 for var i: i32 = 0; i < 5; i = i + 1: total = total + i return total Return Statements return expr returns a value from the current function. Inside none -returning functions, use a bare return , return none , or omit the return statement entirely. Indentation Rules Blocks start after : . The next logical line must be indented by one level (2 spaces in Arx style). Misaligned indentation is treated as a parser error.

text: CSV files and DataFrames Import CSV operations from stdlib.csv . Shared Arrow schemas, batches and IPC remain in stdlib.arrow ; CSV is backed by Arrow C++, not a Python process or a second parser. The native Arrow libraries and a C++ toolchain are required. Read and write a DataFrame ``` title: Copy a CSV file ``` import (read_csv, write_csv) from stdlib.csv fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Read every row and finalize the output ``` var frame: dataframe[...] = read_csv("input.csv") write_csv(frame, "output.csv") return 0 These eager functions close their internal session before returning. Reads return an independent, chunked DataFrame; writes borrow the frame without consuming or mutating it. Temporary inputs such as write_csv(read_csv("input.csv"), "output.csv") are supported. The result must fit in memory: block_size controls parsing blocks, not total memory. Writers return none only after checked finalization. There are no DataFrame .to_* methods or to_* aliases. Never copy a file onto itself using streaming sessions. Parsing policy An omitted schema is inferred from the first block, then frozen. For headerless input, supply a schema or explicit names; names requires header=false and no schema. Projections must be nonempty and unique and preserve requested order. null_values replaces token recognition; an empty list disables it. These choices affect interpretation, not just performance. The eager option schema lives in irx.analysis.table_io ; defaults and validation are implemented by the native CSV options code. Python signatures are in the generated table I/O reference . Stream declarations and contracts live in packages/arx/src/arx/stdlib/csv.x . Arx name/column/token arguments are literal lists, not arbitrary iterable objects. Unknown options and unsupported types fail explicitly. Delimiter, quote and escape bytes must not conflict; NUL, CR and LF are not valid dialect characters. Output quoting uses Arrow's fixed double-quote convention; this is not a complete Python csv dialect engine. CSV projection happens after full input validation and conversion . A bad unselected field still fails. Explicit schemas check header names/order/count and nullability; they control parsing rather than merely asserting types. Checked DataFrame conversion import Schema from stdlib.arrow import read_csv from stdlib.csv # Inside a function: var schema: Schema = Schema() schema.add("id", "int64", nullable=false) var loaded: dataframe[...] = read_csv("ids.csv", schema=schema) var ids: dataframe[id:i64] = cast(loaded, dataframe[id:i64]) Runtime schemas do not infer compile-time column types. The cast above asserts an exact schema; it does not project or coerce data. See the shared checked DataFrame conversion contract for nullability, chunk validation, metadata, and ownership restrictions. CSV supports integer widths, floating point, Boolean, UTF-8/large UTF-8, dates, timestamps and time units. Nested/other unsupported types fail; use Parquet or IPC for those. CSV does not encode type/schema metadata. Supply an explicit schema to preserve widths and temporal units on a roundtrip. Explicit streaming Use CSVStream for incremental processing instead of loading the entire file into a DataFrame. It supports either read or write mode. import CSVStream from stdlib.csv # Inside a function: var source: CSVStream = CSVStream() source.open_read("large.csv") while source.next(): var chunk: dataframe[...] = source.frame() print(chunk.nrows()) source.close() CSVStream() starts closed and has one read or write mode. open_read_as(path, schema, ...) supplies an explicit schema; open_write(path, schema, ...) configures output. These session factories expose delimiter/header and read block size. The additional dialect controls above belong to the eager functions. next() advances; false means EOF, not an empty batch. frame() snapshots the current batch without advancing and survives reader closure. It fails before a successful next() or after EOF. write(frame) and write(batch) require an exact schema. batch() and schema() remain available for Arrow interoperability. Call writer close() explicitly to observe finalization errors; automatic cleanup alone is not proof of success. Wrong-mode access fails, aliases share session state, and failed sessions cannot be reused. The streaming roundtrip example processes every batch. The table example converts CSV to Parquet using only the module-level functions. Text and failure contract UTF-8 and quoted multiline fields are supported. By default only unquoted empty fields are null. Quoted "" remains an empty string; NA and NULL remain text unless configured in null_values . Custom na_rep requires matching read null_values . Non-null unquoted data equal to a null marker is ambiguous; a lossless roundtrip is not guaranteed. Blank one-column rows remain null rows unless explicitly skipped. Malformed record widths fail; skiprows does not enable malformed-row skipping. Headers must be nonempty and unique. Typed header-only input succeeds; completely empty files fail. Inferred null/binary columns need an explicit supported schema or corrected input. CSV has no remote URLs, compression/encoding discovery, append or atomic writes. Validation precedes truncation, but later data/I/O failures can leave partial output. A failed eager read never returns a partial table. Compiled failures use ARX-RUNTIME-ARROW-001 , with typed catchable Arx exceptions. CSV row positions are not invented as Arx source locations. Python integration from irx.table_io import read_csv, write_csv frame = read_csv("input.tsv", delimiter="\t", columns=["id", "name"]) write_csv(frame, "output.csv") These functions return/accept pyarrow.Table , accept string or PathLike paths, and use IRx native sessions/C Stream interchange, not Python format engines. Use pyarrow.Schema for schema . Selectors accept checked sequences. Imports do not compile native code; CSV-only use does not load Parquet, Dataset or Acero. Stale native-library overrides produce a rebuild/unset error. For streaming, irx.record_batch.CSVStream and the lower-level RecordBatchStreamReader.open_csv / RecordBatchStreamWriter.open_csv remain available. Iteration releases its batch on advancement; batch.to_arrow() exports independent Arrow references. Release manually retained batch/schema snapshots explicitly.

text: Data Types Arx uses explicit type annotations for variables, function parameters, and function return types. Type Annotations Function parameters must always be typed. Function return type is declared with -> type and is always required, including -> none . Variable declarations must include an explicit type with var name: type . ``` title: Typed function signature summary: Demonstrates required parameter annotations. ``` fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32: ``` title: add summary: Returns a + b. ``` return a + b Collection annotations Runtime-shaped tensor[T, ...] remains parameter-only; indexed access requires a fixed shape. Runtime-schema dataframe[...] supports locals, aliases, parameters, and returns, but not unchecked named-column access. These are different restrictions. See collections for storage, construction, exact schema casts, and nullable operations. Type Aliases And Union Types Type aliases are top-level declarations. The type word is contextual, so type Name = ... declares an alias while type(value) calls the builtin type-name helper. ``` title: Type alias example summary: Demonstrates a finite numeric union alias. ``` type Number = i32 | i64 fn identity(value: Number) -> Number: ``` title: identity summary: Returns a numeric union value. ``` return value Union annotations use | . Numeric unions currently lower through a shared lossless numeric storage type; incompatible runtime unions are rejected. Generic union bounds constrain template membership without allocating union storage. Runtime tagged unions and runtime narrowing are not part of the current model. Choosing a type See Built-in Types for scalar choices and conversion boundaries. The lexical manifest owns accepted spellings; it is not an API support promise. Class References Declared class names denote identity-preserving, reference-managed object pointers. Local copies and owned returns keep objects alive; final release runs __del__ and drops owned fields. Acyclic instance class/string/file fields are supported, but class values in containers/unions/structs, globals/statics, and generators are rejected. See Classes for construction and lifetime rules; there is no general external ownership ABI.

text: Docstrings Arx docstrings use the Douki YAML format and are validated against the official Douki schema . Docstrings are delimited by triple backticks: ``` title: Example docstring summary: Optional summary value. ``` Supported Targets (Current) module docstring class docstring function docstring method docstring Required Field Every docstring must provide at least: title (required by Douki schema) Valid minimal docstring: ``` title: Add two numbers ``` Module Docstring Rule The module docstring must: be the first top-level statement start at line 1, column 1 (no leading spaces) Valid: ``` title: Module docs ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Entry point for the module. ``` return 1 Function Docstring Rule A function docstring, when present, must be the first statement in the function body, right after : and the required newline/indentation. The parser does not require a docstring in every user function; repository source-contract conventions still apply. Valid: fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Function docs summary: Function summary ``` return 1 Invalid: fn main() -> i32: return 1 ``` title: Too late summary: This docstring is valid Douki but in the wrong position. ``` Class and method docstrings A class docstring may appear as the first item in an indented class body, before fields or methods. Method docstrings follow the same first-body-item rule as function docstrings. Abstract methods can use a docstring-only body so the docstring still belongs to the method block. Current Compiler Behavior Docstrings are currently lexed and validated for: placement rules (module, class, function, and method positions) Douki YAML schema conformance After validation, they are intentionally ignored during AST/IR generation until dedicated DocString nodes are added in astx and irx .

text: Text File I/O File is a builtin reference-managed class for a deliberately small native, POSIX text-file interface. open(...) is a compiler-backed factory adapter to File(...) : both create the same class object through one checked construction path. Both are available without an import and use C stdio, not Python or Arrow. Lowercase file remains a compatibility spelling for the builtin File type. The default is a strict UTF-8 text read. Use mode="w" to create/truncate or mode="a" to append. Only the path and mode can be runtime strings; other Python-shaped settings accept only the implemented default profile. Nondefault buffering, encodings, error policies, newline handling, descriptors, and openers are rejected rather than ignored. Options are checked before I/O; a dynamic mode is checked before opening or truncating a path. Paths are relative to the running program's working directory, not its source file. Reading requires an existing file. Writing creates or truncates it. Appending creates it if necessary and writes at the end. No binary/update/exclusive modes, file descriptors, callbacks, or custom buffering are supported yet. Example Run this in a scratch directory: the example creates/truncates message.txt . ``` title: Native text file example ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main ``` var output: File = File("message.txt", mode="w", encoding="utf-8") var alias: file = output assert alias.write("hello\n") == 6 output.close() alias.close() var source: file = open(file="message.txt") var text: str = source.read() source.close() print(text) return 0 Text and lifetime safety Reads consume all remaining text (not a size-limited chunk), returning an independent string or "" at EOF. CRLF and CR become LF; malformed UTF-8 and embedded NUL fail. Write counts are Unicode characters, not bytes. Explicit flush checks buffered writes without promising durability. Close is idempotent; other operations on a closed file fail. Method signatures and concise contracts live in packages/arx/src/arx/builtins/files.x . Public File values follow ordinary acyclic class-reference ownership. Aliases share one stream and cursor; closing through one reference closes it for all references. References can be reassigned, passed to functions, returned, and stored in class fields. Locals and discarded temporaries release their references on ordinary lexical exits. The last reference releases the native wrapper once, even if the stream was explicitly closed earlier. Read strings own independent memory and can outlive the file. See Classes . Explicit casts to or from builtin File , including identity casts, remain unsupported. Use ordinary assignment to create an alias instead. Construction opens immediately: there is no public unopened constructor, instance open() method, reopening, or builtin subclassing. A default-empty File reference is not an unopened stream; dereferencing it raises the checked class-reference error. Class containers/unions/struct fields, owned globals and statics, generator capture, and external object ownership remain unsupported. The class's native handle is private and uniquely owned. It cannot be extracted, copied, returned, or replaced by user code; NativeFileHandle is not a public Arx type. General class finalization owns its release, not a second manual handle-freeing destructor. Direct creation and I/O failures use ARX-RUNTIME-FILE-001 and raise typed exceptions (including OSError for operating-system failures). Class checks use ARX-RUNTIME-CLASS-001 ; allocation failure remains unrecoverable. Failed creation preserves constructor rollback and completed-base cleanup. See the exception boundary . Explicit close/flush are recommended to observe write errors before later work. with , iteration, seek/tell, binary I/O, and extra file properties are deferred. For explicit imports, use import File as TextFile from builtins.files or import builtins.files as io followed by io.File(...) . These resolve the same canonical class, not an unrelated class with the same name. Existing user or imported File / open bindings retain normal resolution; non-callable local shadowing is an error. The lowercase file type always denotes the builtin. This is a Python-like subset: parameter names/order/default spellings follow Python's interface , but UTF-8 replaces locale-dependent encoding, and NUL-containing text and many optional settings are intentionally unsupported. Existing user/imported functions named open retain normal positional-call resolution. A local non-callable open shadows the builtin and produces an error when called.
title: Text File I/O

text: Functions Functions are defined with fn , a name, parameters in () , and a body after : with indentation. Definition Syntax ``` title: Function definition summary: Shows the structure of a function declaration. ``` fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32: ``` title: add summary: Returns x plus y. ``` return x + y Calling Functions ``` title: Function call example summary: Defines a helper function and calls it from main. ``` fn double(v: i32) -> i32: ``` title: double summary: Returns v multiplied by two. ``` return v * 2 fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Calls double with a constant input. ``` return double(10) Keyword Arguments Ordinary functions and instance/static methods accept named arguments, including through imported aliases and module namespaces: add(y=2, x=1) add(1, y=2) helpers.add(x=1, y=2) counter.read(offset=3) identity<i32>(value=7) Positional arguments must precede keywords. Names are case-sensitive and must match the resolved declaration. Existing ordinary function-call lookup remains module-visible and separate from lexical local-value lookup; builtin/class shadowing rules are unchanged. Duplicate names, positional/name collisions, unknown names, and missing required parameters are compilation errors. A named call may end with a trailing comma. Unpacking ( *args , **kwargs ) and keyword-only/positional-only parameter declarations are not supported. The receiver is evaluated first, then all explicitly supplied values exactly once in source order, even when their names reverse parameter order. Omitted defaults run afterward in parameter declaration order. Unlike Python, Arx already evaluates defaults at call time ; they may reference earlier bound parameters, and method defaults may read self . For f(a, b=a+1, c=b+1) , f(c=9, a=2) calls with (2, 3, 9) and does not evaluate c 's default. Dynamic methods bind names/defaults through the statically selected interface, then dispatch positional values to the override. Fixed extern parameter names can be used; any existing C variadic tail stays positional and uses existing promotions. Keywords do not enable unsupported FFI types. Parser intrinsics and collection operations without a named-call schema still reject keywords. Signature-backed bundled functions such as range(start=0, stop=3) use their declared parameters, not Python overloads. Default Parameter Values Function, method, and extern parameters can declare trailing default values with = . Calls may omit defaulted parameters, including a middle default when a later parameter is supplied by name. ``` title: Default argument example summary: Calls a helper using an optional offset. ``` fn add_offset(value: i32, offset: i32 = 1) -> i32: ``` title: add_offset summary: Adds an optional offset to value. ``` return value + offset fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Uses the declared default offset. ``` return add_offset(4) Template Functions Function templates use an @<...> block on the line immediately before fn . Each template parameter must declare a bound, and bounds may be a single type or a | union of concrete types. Module-local type aliases can name and compose these bounds; importing aliases from another module is not supported. Explicit template arguments are written between the callee name and ( . ``` title: Template function example summary: Uses one bounded template parameter with inferred and explicit calls. ``` type SignedInteger = i8 | i16 | i32 | i64 type Float = f32 | f64 type Real = SignedInteger | Float @<T: Real> fn add(x: T, y: T) -> T: ``` title: add summary: Adds two values that share one template-bound type. ``` return x + y fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Calls template specializations through inference and explicit args. ``` print(add(1, 2)) assert add<f64>(1.5, 2.5) == 4.0 return 0 Here T is one concrete type, not a union-valued argument. Inferred arguments for the same T must agree in type; use explicit specialization or casts to choose conversions. Each concrete member of a bound must support the function body, so define only the numeric group that the operation actually supports. Function Body Rules The block starts after : . The next line must be indented. A function docstring (if present) must be the first element in the function block. Function docstrings must use Douki YAML and include at least title . Example: ``` title: Function docstring placement summary: Function docstring appears as the first body element. ``` fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32: ``` title: Add two numbers summary: Returns x + y. ``` return x + y Extern Prototypes Arx also supports external function declarations: Native package metadata can supply build/link requirements for resolved extern declarations. Calls retain normal parameter/keyword binding; the compiler does not infer a native dependency from a function's name. ``` title: Extern prototype example summary: Declares an external function signature. ``` extern putchard(x: i32) -> i32 Native file construction File and open share checked construction and return ordinary File references. Their restricted native settings are not arbitrary Python keyword forwarding. Class constructors bind keywords through __init__ ; ordinary function/method binding follows the rules above.

text: Calling Functions ``` title: Function call example summary: Defines a helper function and calls it from main. ``` fn double(v: i32) -> i32: ``` title: double summary: Returns v multiplied by two. ``` return v * 2 fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Calls double with a constant input. ``` return double(10)
title: Functions · Calling Functions

text: Keyword Arguments Ordinary functions and instance/static methods accept named arguments, including through imported aliases and module namespaces: add(y=2, x=1) add(1, y=2) helpers.add(x=1, y=2) counter.read(offset=3) identity<i32>(value=7) Positional arguments must precede keywords. Names are case-sensitive and must match the resolved declaration. Existing ordinary function-call lookup remains module-visible and separate from lexical local-value lookup; builtin/class shadowing rules are unchanged. Duplicate names, positional/name collisions, unknown names, and missing required parameters are compilation errors. A named call may end with a trailing comma. Unpacking ( *args , **kwargs ) and keyword-only/positional-only parameter declarations are not supported. The receiver is evaluated first, then all explicitly supplied values exactly once in source order, even when their names reverse parameter order. Omitted defaults run afterward in parameter declaration order. Unlike Python, Arx already evaluates defaults at call time ; they may reference earlier bound parameters, and method defaults may read self . For f(a, b=a+1, c=b+1) , f(c=9, a=2) calls with (2, 3, 9) and does not evaluate c 's default. Dynamic methods bind names/defaults through the statically selected interface, then dispatch positional values to the override. Fixed extern parameter names can be used; any existing C variadic tail stays positional and uses existing promotions. Keywords do not enable unsupported FFI types. Parser intrinsics and collection operations without a named-call schema still reject keywords. Signature-backed bundled functions such as range(start=0, stop=3) use their declared parameters, not Python overloads.
title: Functions · Keyword Arguments

text: Default Parameter Values Function, method, and extern parameters can declare trailing default values with = . Calls may omit defaulted parameters, including a middle default when a later parameter is supplied by name. ``` title: Default argument example summary: Calls a helper using an optional offset. ``` fn add_offset(value: i32, offset: i32 = 1) -> i32: ``` title: add_offset summary: Adds an optional offset to value. ``` return value + offset fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Uses the declared default offset. ``` return add_offset(4)
title: Functions · Default Parameter Values

text: Template Functions Function templates use an @<...> block on the line immediately before fn . Each template parameter must declare a bound, and bounds may be a single type or a | union of concrete types. Module-local type aliases can name and compose these bounds; importing aliases from another module is not supported. Explicit template arguments are written between the callee name and ( . ``` title: Template function example summary: Uses one bounded template parameter with inferred and explicit calls. ``` type SignedInteger = i8 | i16 | i32 | i64 type Float = f32 | f64 type Real = SignedInteger | Float @<T: Real> fn add(x: T, y: T) -> T: ``` title: add summary: Adds two values that share one template-bound type. ``` return x + y fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Calls template specializations through inference and explicit args. ``` print(add(1, 2)) assert add<f64>(1.5, 2.5) == 4.0 return 0 Here T is one concrete type, not a union-valued argument. Inferred arguments for the same T must agree in type; use explicit specialization or casts to choose conversions. Each concrete member of a bound must support the function body, so define only the numeric group that the operation actually supports.
title: Functions · Template Functions

text: Function Body Rules The block starts after : . The next line must be indented. A function docstring (if present) must be the first element in the function block. Function docstrings must use Douki YAML and include at least title . Example: ``` title: Function docstring placement summary: Function docstring appears as the first body element. ``` fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32: ``` title: Add two numbers summary: Returns x + y. ``` return x + y
title: Functions · Function Body Rules

text: Extern Prototypes Arx also supports external function declarations: Native package metadata can supply build/link requirements for resolved extern declarations. Calls retain normal parameter/keyword binding; the compiler does not infer a native dependency from a function's name. ``` title: Extern prototype example summary: Declares an external function signature. ``` extern putchard(x: i32) -> i32
title: Functions · Extern Prototypes

text: Native file construction File and open share checked construction and return ordinary File references. Their restricted native settings are not arbitrary Python keyword forwarding. Class constructors bind keywords through __init__ ; ordinary function/method binding follows the rules above.
title: Functions · Native file construction

text: Getting Started with Arx This guide installs the Arx compiler and compiles a small program. See the compiler CLI for inspection and output modes. Requirements Python 3.10 or newer pip for a published installation, or Mamba/Conda and Poetry for a source checkout LLVM/Clang-compatible tools for object and executable generation a C++ compiler when a program activates native Apache Arrow features Token, ASTx, and most LLVM translation workflows do not invoke the system linker. Building or running an executable does. Install from PyPI pip install arxlang arx --version The arxlang distribution installs the arx Python package and the arx command. Its IRx dependency provides the analysis, LLVM, and native runtime layers. Install a development checkout git clone https://github.com/arxlang/arx.git cd arx mamba env create --file conda/dev.yaml conda activate arx poetry install The repository is a monorepo containing Arx, ASTx, IRx, ArxPy, ArxJIT, and the low-profile AIX experiment. Compile a program Create hello.x : ``` title: Hello module summary: Compiles a small typed Arx program. ``` fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32: ``` title: add summary: Adds two values. ``` return a + b fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Prints one result and returns success. ``` print(add(20, 22)) return 0 Inspect the compiler stages: arx --show-tokens hello.x arx --show-ast hello.x arx --show-llvm-ir hello.x Build and run: arx hello.x --output-file hello ./hello # Equivalent one-step forms arx --run hello.x arx run hello.x An executable normally defines main() -> i32 and returns 0 on success. A single main(n: i32) parameter follows the native C main ABI and receives argc . Compile an Arrow-backed value Arx tensors, DataFrames, and Series activate IRx's native Apache Arrow C++ runtime: ``` title: Arrow-backed collections summary: Uses a Tensor, DataFrame, and Series. ``` fn main() -> i32: var grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] var rows: dataframe[id: i32, score: f64] = dataframe({ id: [1, 2, 3], score: [0.5, 0.8, 1.0], }) var scores: series[f64] = rows.score assert grid[1, 0] == 3 assert rows.nrows() == 3 assert scores[2] == 1.0 return 0 The corresponding native runtime sources and linker inputs are included only when the compilation unit uses those features. Exchange Arrow data with Python stdlib.arrow adds runtime-schema RecordBatches, IPC file/stream readers and writers, and TCP clients. No new language syntax or Python serialization is needed in the Arx producer. C++20 and the installed Arrow libraries are required at build/link time. From a checkout, run all compiled interoperability examples: python examples/arrow/run.py --directory .tmp/arrow-demo See the Arrow interoperability guide for schema types, nullable values, C Data/C Stream ownership and network limitations. Next steps Compiler CLI Language syntax Language reference Projects and imports Compiled tests Apache Arrow runtime Workflow guides Text files : shared references, checked UTF-8, and explicit close. Run examples/file-io.x in a scratch directory; it creates or truncates its output file. Classes : identity, construction, and final-reference cleanup. CSV and Parquet : eager DataFrames or explicit bounded streams, exact schema checks, and safe output publication. Nullable collections : validity, checked arithmetic, and mutation ownership. Native packages : explicit external C ABI dependencies. The complete programs above are compiled and run from this page by packages/arx/tests/python/test_documentation.py .
title: Getting Started with Arx

text: Arx Programming Language Independent libraries can use native package dependencies to link C ABI backends without adding domain-specific runtime features to Arx. Arx is the programming language and source frontend in the ArxLang ecosystem. The arxlang distribution provides the arx Python package and the arx command-line compiler. Arx owns source syntax, lexing, parsing, project-aware imports, compiler CLI behavior, and compiled tests. The parser emits ASTx nodes. IRx then performs semantic analysis, LLVM lowering, native runtime activation, and artifact generation. Arx source -> Arx lexer and parser -> ASTx nodes -> IRx semantic analysis -> LLVM IR -> object file or executable Status: Arx is a functional prototype. Implemented behavior is tested, but the language and compiler interfaces are not production-stable. text: Modules A module in Arx is a source file (for example, math.x ) containing top-level statements such as imports, function definitions, and extern declarations. Module Layout ``` title: Math module example summary: Module with one documented function. ``` fn average(x: f32, y: f32) -> f32: ``` title: average summary: Returns the arithmetic mean of x and y. ``` return (x + y) * 0.5 Package Layout When a project uses the default src/ source root, or declares [build].src_dir , Arx treats files under that source root as package modules addressed by dotted names. Example project layout: . ├── .arxproject.toml ├── src │ └── geometry │ ├── __init__.x │ ├── shared │ │ └── math.x │ └── shapes │ ├── area.x │ └── helpers.x └── tests └── test_area.x With the default src/ source root: src/geometry/__init__.x is module geometry src/geometry/shared/math.x is module geometry.shared.math src/geometry/shapes/area.x is module geometry.shapes.area src/geometry/shapes/helpers.x is module geometry.shapes.helpers Use __init__.x as the package root, following the same layout idea as Python packages. Import Syntax import geometry.shapes.area import geometry.shapes.area as area import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area import circle_area as area_of_circle from geometry.shapes.area import (circle_area, square_area) from geometry.shapes.area import radius_to_diameter from .helpers import (circle_area, square_area) from .area import clamp from ..shared.math Rules: Import statements are module-level statements. Grouped imports use parentheses. Grouped imports require from . Trailing commas are allowed in grouped imports. Empty grouped imports are invalid. Absolute module paths use dotted notation. Relative imports are supported only with from imports. Relative imports use one or more leading dots before the module path. Plain relative module imports such as import .area are not supported yet. Prefer from imports when you want callable declarations without a module qualifier. Absolute Imports Use absolute dotted paths for public imports across package boundaries: import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area Installed Package Imports Arx can also resolve absolute imports from installed Arx source packages declared in [project].dependencies in .arxproject.toml . For example, if the current project declares an installed dependency that exposes a package root named local_lib , this import resolves from that installed package when no local project source shadows it: import sum2 from local_lib.stats Installed package lookup is scoped to the current Python environment running arx . The compiler reads installed distribution metadata, follows transitive dependency metadata, and uses packaged .arxproject.toml files to find Arx source roots. It does not install packages, access the network, or change generated IR/codegen behavior. For installed packages with the normal project layout, place .arxproject.toml at the packaged project root and declare both [build].src_dir and [build].package : site-packages/local_lib_project/ ├── .arxproject.toml └── src └── local_lib ├── __init__.x └── stats.x [build] src_dir = "src" package = "local_lib" With that layout, local_lib.stats resolves to site-packages/local_lib_project/src/local_lib/stats.x . Flat package layouts are also supported for packages that place .arxproject.toml and .x files directly in the package directory: site-packages/local_lib/ ├── .arxproject.toml ├── __init__.x └── stats.x Resolution precedence is: local/current project source files installed Arx dependency packages unresolved import error The reserved stdlib and internal builtins namespaces always remain owned by the compiler and cannot be replaced by installed packages. Bundled stdlib Arx ships a first-party standard library namespace called stdlib . stdlib is bundled inside the installed arx Python package stdlib modules are written in Arx; stdlib.arrow also binds the registered IRx RecordBatch native runtime stdlib modules are resolved from the installed package location, not from the user project directory local user modules are not allowed to shadow the reserved stdlib namespace Example: import math from stdlib fn main() -> i32: return math.square(4) + math.clamp(0 - 3, 0, 2) Bundled builtins Compiler-provided builtins live in bundled .x package resources, separately from the importable stdlib . They are not copied into user projects, and local sources cannot replace the reserved namespace. Ambient names are injected only when not shadowed by a declaration or import. Explicit builtins.files imports resolve the canonical File class , not a second implementation. Builtin range currently allocates a scalar list; its declaration lives in packages/arx/src/arx/builtins/generators.x . See for-in workflows and list ownership . The module name does not imply Arx supports general generators or yield . Namespace Imports Use a module alias when you want to keep names grouped under a module namespace: ``` title: Geometry namespace import summary: Call one module member through a namespace alias. ``` import geometry.shapes.area as area fn main() -> f64: ``` title: main summary: Demonstrates namespace member access. ``` return area.circle_area(10.0) Direct symbol imports remain available when you prefer shorter local names: import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area Relative Imports Use relative from imports for package-internal references. For example, inside geometry.shapes.area : import radius_to_diameter from .helpers import clamp from ..shared.math Module Docstring Arx supports module docstrings in Douki YAML format, delimited by triple backticks: ``` title: Module documentation summary: Optional summary text ``` Current placement rule: The module docstring must be the first top-level element in the file. It must begin at character 0 of line 1 (no leading spaces). Valid: ``` title: Module docs ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Entry point for the module. ``` return 1 Invalid (leading indentation before module docstring): ``` title: Module docs ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Entry point for the module. ``` return 1 For now, module docstrings are parsed and validated but ignored by AST/IR generation. stdlib.arrow exports Schema , BatchBuilder , RecordBatch , IPCReader and IPCWriter . It uses ordinary classes and nominal opaque native handles, not new keywords. See the Arrow API and examples . Native bindings are supplied only for the bundled reserved module; a user module cannot gain these bindings merely by declaring matching handle type names. Tabular standard-library modules stdlib.csv : read_csv , write_csv , and the unified streaming CSVStream owner. stdlib.parquet : read_parquet , write_parquet , ParquetStream , ParquetOptions , ParquetFilter , and where . stdlib.arrow : canonical shared Schema , RecordBatch , BatchBuilder , IPC and Arrow interoperability. Format classes are not exported from stdlib.arrow . Import shared types from that canonical module rather than through a format module. Namespace-qualified calls and explicit aliases work normally. Format functions are not global builtins, and equally named user functions receive no native privileges. CSV/shared Arrow do not activate the optional Parquet feature.

text: External Native Packages Arx libraries can ship C ABI wrappers alongside their .x sources. The compiler discovers them through normal project dependencies and links declared native features from the reachable module graph. No Python plugins or shell build hooks run during discovery. Source-only manifests are unchanged. For example, an external rendering backend can receive numeric coordinates, UTF-8 labels, and a filename and write JPEG itself. This adds no chart API or JPEG codec to Arx and does not require binary Arx File support. Manifest and distribution [project] name = "demo-native" version = "0.1.0" [build] package = "demo_native" src_dir = "src" [native] version = 1 [native.features.backend] libraries = ["m"] [[native.features.backend.artifacts]] kind = "c_source" path = "native/shim.c" include_dirs = ["native/include"] [native.modules."demo_native.bridge"] features = ["backend"] This layout contains .arxproject.toml , src/demo_native/__init__.x , src/demo_native/bridge.x , native/shim.c , and native/include/ . Include all resources in the wheel/sdist, preserving manifest-relative paths. Consumers declare the distribution in project.dependencies , install it externally, then import its modules normally. Local development uses the same contract. Version 1 supports c_source , cxx_source , object , and static_library . Source compilation requires the appropriate toolchain; objects/archives must match the target ABI. Optional system library names become individual -l arguments. The compiler never installs missing headers/libraries or downloads dependencies. Arbitrary shell hooks and compiler flags are not accepted. Absolute/traversing paths, escaping symlinks, missing inputs, unknown fields, unsupported versions/features, and invalid library names are errors. Modules must belong to the package's actual origin. Local shadow modules cannot inherit installed native capabilities, and features cannot override builtins. Mappings apply to actual top-level extern declarations, not ordinary functions or callee spellings. C symbols must match the extern names; use unique prefixes. Incompatible ABI/native requirements are rejected across modules. Reachable extern declarations may activate features even if never called; this is not call-site dead-code elimination. Unrelated installed packages add no inputs. C ABI and ownership The first route uses existing scalar/string extern support.
