text: Parquet files and DataFrames Import operations from stdlib.parquet , independently of CSV. Shared Schema / RecordBatch and IPC remain in stdlib.arrow . All file operations use the native Arrow/Parquet engine; compiled programs do not start Python. Read and write a DataFrame ``` title: Filter and copy Parquet rows ``` import (read_parquet, write_parquet, where) from stdlib.parquet fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Filter exact rows and finalize the destination ``` var frame: dataframe[...] = read_parquet("events.parquet", columns=["name"], filters=where("id", ">", 10)) write_parquet(frame, "selected.parquet", compression="zstd", atomic=true) return 0 Reads eagerly return an independently owned, chunked DataFrame and close the reader. Writes borrow their input and return none only after checked finalization. The full result must fit in memory; batch_size is not a total memory limit. No RecordBatch conversion or DataFrame .to_* method is required. Writes are non-atomic by default and do not append unless requested. Choose atomic publication explicitly when existing output must survive a failed write; see the safe-write contract for its limits. Option declarations and validation live in irx.analysis.table_io , irx.parquet_options , and packages/arx/src/arx/stdlib/parquet.x . The generated Python reference supplies Python signatures; the workflow and safety rules below apply to the native engine. Explicit keywords override an options snapshot even when equal to a default . Selections and filters replace, not append to, the corresponding settings. The options owner is never mutated. Unknown parameters, empty selections and unsupported values fail rather than falling back. Without options , reads inspect the path, treating files as files and directories as Hive-aware datasets; suffixes are irrelevant. Writes with partition_columns select Hive dataset mode. Explicit options preserves its existing dataset/Hive policy instead of enabling discovery automatically. Typed predicates and configuration import (ParquetFilter, ParquetOptions, where) from stdlib.parquet # Inside a function; minimum_id may be a runtime signed integer: var predicate: ParquetFilter = where("id", ">=", minimum_id) var both: ParquetFilter = predicate.and_where("active", "==", true) var options: ParquetOptions = ParquetOptions(atomic=true, durable=true) Comparisons are == , != , < , <= , > , >= , with string, signed integer, floating or Boolean values. where("name", "is_null") and is_valid omit the value. and_where returns a separate group, preserving the original. Filter columns need not be projected; nulls are excluded by ordinary comparisons. Pruning is only an optimization, never a substitute for filtering rows. OR/IN, serialized type tags and tuple-filter expressions are not this public API. Explicit streaming and ownership Use ParquetStream for incremental reading or writing. It starts closed and has one active mode. Reads advance with next() ; false means EOF, not an empty batch, and leaves the reader open. Current batch/frame snapshots require a successful advance and survive reader closure. Schema snapshots are independent, even before the first batch or after EOF. Writers require an exact input schema, including metadata and nullability. Schema snapshots describe that input; explicit normalization may change the physical schema on disk. Multiple writes may share a buffered row group. Call writer close() explicitly to check footer finalization. Successful close is idempotent and permits reopening; a failed session allows cleanup only. Aliases share session state. Wrong-mode calls fail before opening another file. Compiled runtime failures use ARX-RUNTIME-ARROW-001 , with typed catchable Arx exceptions. Batch and row-group sizes must be positive; batching bounds rows and normal buffering, not total bytes in arbitrary values or retained frames. See the basic roundtrip and nullable-data scan examples. Configured sessions Arx exposes a scoped ParquetOptions builder. Its validated setters are copied at open; later mutations do not change an active session: import (ParquetStream, ParquetOptions, where) from stdlib.parquet # Inside a function: var options: ParquetOptions = ParquetOptions(batch_size=1024) options.set_text("column", "name") options.set_filters(where("id", ">", 10)) var source: ParquetStream = ParquetStream() source.open_read_options("input.parquet", options) Use open_write_options(path, schema, options) for writes. Unknown settings and wrong-mode settings fail rather than being ignored. Python accepts an immutable ParquetOptions value via open_read(..., options=...) or open_write(..., options=...) ; explicit convenience arguments override the snapshot, including explicit defaults. Python None means no override. Arx streaming uses the explicit open_*_options methods for advanced settings. Projection and row-group selection preserve requested order; row groups are file-only. Arx set_text("column", ...) and set_int("row_group", ...) add selections, while eager keyword selections replace the captured selection. Python uses checked tuples for selections and predicates. Neither surface is a general query language. Invalid codecs, settings, or mode combinations fail explicitly. Types and temporal policy RecordBatch I/O supports: signed/unsigned integers of 8/16/32/64 bits, f32 , f64 , Boolean; UTF-8/large UTF-8, binary/large binary/fixed-size binary; decimal128/decimal256, null-typed fields; date32 , timestamp[ms/us/ns] including timezones, time32[ms] , time64[us/ns] ; recursively nested lists, large/fixed lists, structs and maps; Arrow dictionaries with string or binary values; native registered extensions with supported storage (tested with UUID/JSON); opaque application/Python extension storage with exact Arrow extension metadata. Native code does not execute Python extension callbacks. Python consumers can reconstruct an extension after registering its implementation. Nulls, type parameters, field order, child names, timezones and user metadata are retained. Dictionary codebooks/codes can be reorganized across batches; do not treat dictionary indices as stable application identifiers. Names must be nonempty, unique among siblings, valid UTF-8 and NUL-free. ARROW:schema is reserved. Zero-column schemas and unsupported types fail explicitly. The writer uses Parquet 2.6 and embedded Arrow schemas. Nested child names are preserved rather than replaced with element . Other Parquet consumers may ignore Arrow metadata. UTF-8 values containing NUL survive C Data/file I/O, but the Arx scalar string getter cannot represent them. Strict mode rejects date64 , timestamp[s] and time32[s] on write. normalize=true explicitly converts them to date32 , timestamp[ms] and time32[ms] , including nested fields. Safe casts reject overflow and truncation: for example, a date64 value not aligned to a whole day fails. The reader reports the physical normalized type, not an invented original type. Extension storage is never implicitly normalized. Explicit logical reconstruction reconstruct=true on a file or dataset writer supports numeric dictionaries (including decimals) and fixed-size lists with null parents. IRx writes ordinary value columns/variable lists plus the reserved IRX:logical_schema:v1 IPC schema metadata. IRx readers validate that metadata against the physical schema and restore the logical types automatically, including nested fields and projected scans. Dictionary codebooks are rebuilt per batch; safe index casts reject capacity overflow. Ordered dictionary reconstruction is rejected because its codebook ordering cannot be preserved. Codes are not stable identifiers. Dataset common metadata carries the logical schema across fragments, including projection and atomic append. Reconstruction does not relax append schema checks; schema evolution that changes logical-schema metadata is rejected. Other readers see the documented physical types, not the reconstructed schema. Use IPC when arbitrary consumers must see the exact original Arrow types. Strict writes without this option still reject numeric dictionaries and null fixed-list parents. Unions and list views are not supported; errors are explicit. Both internal schema metadata keys are reserved. The scalar BatchBuilder /getter API is not a recursive value API; use C Data imports and RecordBatch.from_arrow / to_arrow for rich values. Datasets, evolution and filesystems Set dataset=true for a directory scan and hive=true for name=value partitions. Every fragment schema is inspected. Default mode requires matching physical schemas. unify=true unions compatible fields and materializes missing values as null. Fields missing from any fragment must be declared nullable; conflicting physical types fail, without implicit widening. Union schemas retain the first-seen user metadata rather than merging conflicting metadata. Expected schemas remain assertions against the final projected scan schema. Dataset writes require dataset=true , hive=true , and partition_columns . Each input batch is written as bounded, independently finalized fragments with fresh names. At least one non-partition column is required. _common_metadata records the full schema, preserving original partition types and allowing empty datasets. Ordinary writes require append=true for an existing destination and an exact stored schema. They may leave completed fragments after a later error. For transactional output use atomic=true on a local POSIX filesystem. IRx creates immutable generations in a hidden sibling .<name>.irx-versions directory and atomically switches the public dataset symlink on successful close. IRx readers pin one generation at open, so existing readers retain a consistent view during replacement. Only new destinations or managed snapshot symlinks are accepted, not existing ordinary directories. Subsequent writes to a snapshot must also use atomic=true . Snapshot append retains old fragments and adds new ones. With append=true , atomic=true , unify=true , incoming schemas can add or omit nullable fields; shared fields must have identical types, nullability and metadata. There is no implicit widening or required-field synthesis. Read evolved datasets with unify=true . Existing immutable fragments are hardlinked, not rewritten. Old generations are deliberately retained for active readers. There is no automatic garbage collector: remove unreachable generations only after all readers have closed. Never edit a published generation or its hardlinked files. External readers can follow the public symlink, but only IRx readers implement generation pinning. This is a local commit protocol, not an object-store table format or distributed transaction. Decimal128/256 and floating-point partition keys preserve their declared types. Decimal paths are parsed with checked Arrow decimal conversion rather than floating-point intermediates. Floating keys must be finite and cannot be negative zero: equality grouping cannot preserve those values exactly. Hive names cannot contain / , backslash, = or % . The string value __HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__ is reserved for nulls. Other strings are URI-escaped. Recorded schemas preserve partition types, column order and metadata. Paths and URIs use Arrow's filesystem implementations. Local paths and file:// are tested; cloud schemes work only when the installed Arrow build and its credential providers support them. Unsupported backends fail, never fall back to a local filename. Live cloud-provider integration is not covered by local tests. Use credential providers, not credentials embedded in paths or source code. Encryption and safe writes File and dataset encryption use Parquet AES footer-key encryption. Each dataset fragment gets fresh encryption properties; the schema footer is encrypted too. Python accepts ParquetOptions(encryption_key=key_bytes) with a 16/24/32-byte key. Arx accepts options.encryption_key_hex(runtime_key) with 32/48/64 hexadecimal digits. Use runtime-provided secrets; never commit real keys in examples or source. The same key is needed to read encrypted data. Missing/wrong keys fail. Native option copies use Arrow's secure string storage; caller-owned Python/Arx values remain the caller's responsibility. KMS integration, rotation and per-column keys are outside this interface. atomic=true writes a securely created sibling temporary file and replaces the destination only after successful finalization. Abandoning a Python context or releasing an unfinished writer does not commit it. Single-file append=true streams the existing file into a new temporary output and then adds new batches; it never concatenates Parquet files. Both operations currently require a local POSIX filesystem . Local writers hold a nonblocking advisory lock for their entire session, including the old-data read in append. A second cooperating writer fails with a busy error before truncation. Locks are released on close, abort, failure or process death. Hidden lock files are intentionally persistent; do not delete them while writers may exist. Coordination is by canonical path, not hardlink identity, and does not exclude non-IRx writers. durable=true requires atomic replacement or file rewrite append. It fsyncs completed data and directories before/after publication. A failure after publication (for example the final directory fsync) can report an error while the new data is already visible; its durability is then uncertain. Abrupt process death can leave unpublished temporaries/generations. Durability still depends on the local filesystem/device honoring fsync. Without atomic mode, later I/O failures can leave partial output. Options/schema validation precedes truncation, but data-dependent failures cannot all be detected at open time. Missing codecs fail instead of falling back. Batching bounds normal buffering, not bytes consumed by arbitrarily large values or file metadata. DataFrame conversion Use the shared checked conversion contract and parameterized schema rules . A static cast is an exact assertion, never implicit physical conversion or projection. Runtime-schema frames preserve supported rich Arrow data without inferring static column types. Format normalization/reconstruction rules above still apply when those frames are written to Parquet. Python example from irx.table_io import read_parquet, write_parquet, where from irx.record_batch import ParquetOptions frame = read_parquet("input.parquet", columns=["name"], filters=where("id", ">", 10)) write_parquet(frame, "output.parquet", compression="zstd", options=ParquetOptions(atomic=True)) These helpers return/accept pyarrow.Table , accept PathLike paths and pyarrow.Schema assertions, and use the native C Stream bridge. No Python format engine is substituted. For streaming, irx.record_batch.ParquetStream remains available. Its iteration releases a batch on advancement. Use next_batch() and explicit release() when retaining the native batch longer; exported to_arrow() values own independent references. Low-level open_parquet factories remain available. Import does not build native code. CSV/IPC use the base ctypes library; Parquet loads a separate on-demand plugin linked to that same base instance. IRX_RECORD_BATCH_LIBRARY overrides retain the legacy all-in-one ABI contract. IRx registers parquet separately from record_batch . The base feature links Arrow and Compute for nullable kernels. Parquet additionally links matching Parquet, Dataset and Acero libraries. Arx resolves the canonical bundled modules, but lowers only resolved reachable declarations (whole referenced classes, including destructors). CSV-only programs no longer activate or link Parquet.

No Python format engine is substituted. For streaming, irx.record_batch.ParquetStream remains available. Its iteration releases a batch on advancement. Use next_batch() and explicit release() when retaining the native batch longer; exported to_arrow() values own independent references. Low-level open_parquet factories remain available. Import does not build native code. CSV/IPC use the base ctypes library; Parquet loads a separate on-demand plugin linked to that same base instance. IRX_RECORD_BATCH_LIBRARY overrides retain the legacy all-in-one ABI contract. IRx registers parquet separately from record_batch . The base feature links Arrow and Compute for nullable kernels. Parquet additionally links matching Parquet, Dataset and Acero libraries. Arx resolves the canonical bundled modules, but lowers only resolved reachable declarations (whole referenced classes, including destructors). CSV-only programs no longer activate or link Parquet.

text: Arx Projects and Imports The Arx compiler can read project metadata from .arxproject.toml . The compiler uses this metadata for source layout, import resolution, output defaults, and test discovery. ArxPM provides higher-level project and environment workflows. Project layout A conventional source tree is: . ├── .arxproject.toml ├── src │ └── geometry │ ├── __init__.x │ ├── shared │ │ └── math.x │ └── shapes │ ├── area.x │ └── helpers.x └── tests └── test_area.x Manifest [project] name = "geometry" version = "0.1.0" requires-arx = ">=1.0,<2" dependencies = [ "sciarx>=0.0.3,<1", ] [environment] kind = "conda" name = "geometry" [build-system] dependencies = [ "arxlang>=1.0,<2", ] [build] src_dir = "src" out_dir = "build" package = "geometry" requires-arx uses standard version-specifier syntax. Project dependencies use standard requirement strings and may also be direct references. The compiler validates the manifest but does not install dependencies during import resolution. Use ArxPM or another environment tool to provision them. Imports import geometry.shapes.area import geometry.shapes.area as area import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area import circle_area as area_of_circle from geometry.shapes.area import (circle_area, square_area) from geometry.shapes.area import helper from .helpers import clamp from ..shared.math Relative imports require the from form. Plain import .area is not supported. The resolver checks local project modules before installed Arx packages. The compiler reserves: stdlib for bundled Arx modules, including native-backed Arrow APIs builtins for compiler-injected source modules import math from stdlib fn main() -> i32: return math.square(4) Build settings Libraries may bind native artifacts and system libraries to their own extern modules. See External Native Packages for versioned metadata, package-relative paths, distribution layout, and the C ABI contract. The [build] table can select: src_dir : source root package : default package/module root out_dir : build output directory mode : project build mode when supported by the invoking tool The arx command compiles an entry file and resolves its imported module graph. ArxPM owns workspace-level commands such as project initialization, dependency installation, build, run, packaging, and publishing. Test settings The optional [tests] table controls compiled test discovery: [tests] paths = ["tests", "integration"] exclude = ["tests/experimental_*.x"] file_pattern = "test_*.x" function_pattern = "test_*" See Compiled Tests for the test function contract and CLI flags.

text: Arx Preview Contracts These safety and compatibility decisions describe the non-stable 2026-preview edition (language draft 0.1.0 ). They are not a complete language specification. The capability matrix is the single support summary; executable conformance lives in the compiler tests. Arithmetic and evaluation Boolean evaluation && and || require Boolean operands. The left operand is evaluated first. For lhs && rhs , rhs is evaluated only when lhs is true . For lhs || rhs , rhs is evaluated only when lhs is false . packages/arx/tests/arx/test_datatypes.x contains the black-box conformance case: the skipped operand deliberately asserts false. IRx also verifies that lowering uses conditional blocks and a merge value rather than eager LLVM and / or instructions. Fixed-width integer overflow Fixed-width signed and unsigned 8–64-bit integer + , - , * , negation, and supported increment/decrement operations are checked in every build. IRx fixed-width range induction is checked too; the stdlib range helper uses wider endpoint arithmetic to terminate safely on an overshooting step. Overflow fails before storing or publishing a result; an unused expression is still checked. Provably evaluated invalid constant operations are semantic errors. Untaken branches and short-circuited operands do not execute checks. Implicit numeric conversions preserve the entire source type's domain . Mixed operands use the smallest supported lossless common domain: i32 + u32 computes in i64 , and i32 + f32 in f64 ; i64 + u64 and i64 + f64 require an explicit conversion. A destination annotation never widens a computation retroactively. Same-type templates keep their selected type; widen operands or select math.square<i64>(narrow) before multiplication, not afterward. Source integer literals use the declared/argument/peer type when representable, otherwise default to i32 , then i64 . Uncontextualized floating literals default to f32 . Decimal literals retain their exact value until type selection, then round directly to the chosen binary format, nearest with ties to even. Explicitly typed ASTx literals are never recontextualized. Generic inference uses concrete arguments before contextualizing literal arguments, independently of argument order; literals do not make conflicting concrete same- T arguments compatible. cast(value, Type) checks integer range, including equal-width signedness changes. Float-to-integer casts truncate toward zero, then require a finite, representable result. Explicit integer-to-float and float-narrowing casts may round; finite input must not become infinity. Existing floating NaN, infinity, signed zero, and ordinary IEEE floating arithmetic are preserved. Implicit integer-to-float conversions may not discard integer precision. Intentional modulo arithmetic requires wrapping_add , wrapping_sub , wrapping_mul , or wrapping_cast(value, IntegerType) . Binary wrapping operands must have the same integer type, or an explicit lossless specialization such as wrapping_add<i64>(narrow, 1) . Boolean and floating operands are rejected. These forms do not change surrounding expressions' checked behavior. Integer division and remainder failures Signed integer division truncates toward zero. Division and remainder reject zero divisors and signed minimum with negative one before LLVM executes the operation. Integer SIMD lowering checks every supplied active lane; no masked source-vector API is implied. Floating-point division follows IEEE behavior. Dynamic integer zero divisors raise ZeroDivisionError ; out-of-range arithmetic and conversions raise OverflowError , at every optimization level. Diagnostic codes remain ARX-RUNTIME-ARITHMETIC-001 and ARX-RUNTIME-CONVERSION-001 . These failures propagate through generated cleanup edges and can be caught; uncaught exceptions produce structured reports and a nonzero exit status. Statically invalid expressions remain compile-time diagnostics. See the exception support boundary . Nullable and Series arithmetic retains checked Arrow kernels, status checking, null propagation, and checked reduction accumulators. Nullable scalar casts skip invalid payloads entirely. Tensor element operations use scalar checks; bulk tensor arithmetic and nonidentity Series/tensor casts are rejected rather than reinterpreting storage. List length/search results must fit their public i32 domain. Numeric runtime unions require lossless shared storage; generic union bounds are membership constraints and need no runtime storage. Raw FFI internals and external native functions remain outside these language guarantees. Ownership The runtime ownership contract owns the detailed create/borrow/move/release rules for lists, strings, files, and class references. Dynamic lists are move-only and cleaned up on ordinary lexical exits, not process-lifetime allocations. Shared class references follow a different model. Use the class lifecycle guide for construction and field ownership, and the file guide for shared cursor and close behavior. IRx cleanup paths for break / continue or generators do not establish Arx source support for those constructs. Fatal errors do not generally unwind caller frames. Do not depend on automatic cleanup to confirm successful writer finalization; follow the CSV or Parquet close contract. Modules and failures Module graph failures One entry module identifies a compiler-owned, canonical dependency graph. Missing modules are IRX-S011 failures and import cycles are IRX-S012 failures; a cycle is never executed or initialized partially. A canonical module is resolved and analyzed once per compilation session. Module-level runtime initialization order remains outside the stable subset until Arx admits and specifies executable module-level statements. Compiler and process failures Expected source/compiler failures exit the CLI with status 1, CLI usage failures use status 2, and sanitized internal compiler failures use status 70. --traceback is an explicit developer opt-in. Compiled assertions raise AssertionError . Uncaught exceptions emit ARX_EXCEPTION records with stable operation codes and ARX_EXCEPTION_FRAME records for recorded call sites, then exit nonzero. The test runner and ArxPy decode these reports without treating completed subprocess failures as Python compiler errors. Unrecoverable native or exception-machinery allocation failures retain the ARX_RUNTIME_FAIL fallback; they do not promise recovery or cleanup. Compatibility identifiers language draft: 0.1.0 ; source edition: 2026-preview ; compiler diagnostic JSON schema: 1 ; RecordBatch native C ABI: 2 . The language draft and preview edition do not grant source compatibility. Before Arx 2.0, replace APIs within the requested scope and update callers, tests, source contracts, and necessary guides together. Record intentional breaking changes in concise release notes rather than parallel deprecated API documentation. Native ABI producers and consumers must remain aligned. Diagnostics contract Stable compiler failures will have a code, phase, message, and a trustworthy optional source location. Normal CLI use renders expected Arx and IRx failures without a Python traceback and exits nonzero. Unexpected internal failures are not relabeled as user errors. The source loader emits ARX-SOURCE-* , the lexer emits ARX-LEX-* , the parser emits ARX-PARSE-* , and IRx formats its diagnostic families as IRX-* . --diagnostic-format json emits schema version 1 for structured compiler-phase failures. The complete stable-code catalog remains GA work; schema versions must be checked rather than inferred. Decisions still required A stable specification still needs floating-point non-finite/NaN and narrowing rules, broader Unicode operations, general resource/error propagation, FFI and artifact guarantees, and a versioned conformance suite. Do not promote a preview behavior to a compatibility promise without that evidence. At Arx 2.0, explicitly define source/package/native ABI compatibility, edition changes, any deprecation policy, supported toolchains, and release support periods. The pre-2.0 policy must not silently continue afterward.
title: Arx Preview Contracts

text: Arx Lexical Syntax The authoritative token spellings, aliases, and editor-tooling inventory live in packages/arx/src/arx/lexer/syntax.json . This guide covers writing source and important restrictions, not a duplicate token catalog. Parser and semantic support is summarized in the capability matrix . Source files and whitespace recognized extensions: .x and .arx indentation is significant the canonical indentation unit is 2 spaces tabs outside quoted literal contents are rejected; use spaces newlines delimit logical lines blank lines do not create indentation transitions Files must be valid UTF-8 and no larger than 4 MiB of UTF-8 bytes. Token start locations use one-based lines and Unicode code-point columns. The lexer also limits delimiter nesting to 256, numeric tokens to 4,096 characters, and non-EOF tokens to 250,000. These are compiler-version resource limits, not a frozen language compatibility promise. fn absolute(value: i32) -> i32: if value < 0: return 0 - value else: return value Comments and docstrings # starts a line comment. Block comments are not supported. Triple backticks delimit Douki YAML docstrings and produce a dedicated docstring token: ``` title: Module documentation summary: Optional description. ``` Docstring placement and schema validation are parser concerns documented in Docstrings . Identifiers Identifiers start with a Unicode letter or _ and continue with Unicode alphanumeric characters or _ . Reference pattern for Unicode-aware tooling: (?:[_\p{L}])(?:[_\p{L}\p{N}])* The exact Unicode categories currently follow the Python runtime. Matching is case-sensitive. Reserved forms Lexical reservation does not promise parsing or lowering. In particular, general const , then , and operator declarations remain unavailable even though their spellings are recognized. Numeric literals Supported forms: decimal integers: 0 , 42 decimal floats with one dot: 3.14 , .5 , 5. Not supported: hexadecimal, binary, or octal prefixes exponent notation such as 1e9 separators such as 1_000 literal suffixes such as 42u32 Multiple dots are invalid, and . by itself is punctuation rather than a number. Strings and characters Double quotes create string literals. Single quotes create character literals. The lexer recognizes these escapes: Escape Value \\ backslash \n newline \r carriage return \t tab \" double quote \' single quote Raw strings, triple-quoted strings, and interpolation are not supported. Triple backticks are reserved for Douki docstrings, not ordinary string values. Structural forms Declaration modifiers @[public, static, constant] version: i32 = 1 Recognized modifiers are public , private , protected , static , constant , mutable , abstract , and extern . Templates @<T: i32 | f64> fn identity(value: T) -> T: return value Explicit template calls use angle brackets: identity<f64>(1.5) . Imports Grouped imports use parentheses, require from , and allow a trailing comma: import ( sin, cos, tan as tangent, ) from math Collection annotations See type annotations . Literal ellipsis has different support boundaries for runtime-shaped tensors and runtime-schema DataFrames; it is not uniformly parameter-only. Consistency rule Changes to lexical syntax update the manifest first, then tokenization, parser, tests, and derived editor consumers. Update this short guide only for changed workflows or restrictions. File , open , and dunder method names remain identifiers, not new keywords. Class lifecycle hooks do not add Arx with statements. Named calls use resolved signatures, not lexical privilege based on the callee's spelling.

text: Compiled Tests arx test discovers Arx test functions, compiles each selected test into an executable, and runs it in a separate subprocess. Test files and functions The default discovery rules are: search the tests directory include files matching test_*.x include functions matching test_* require zero parameters and a none return type Test entry files must not define main , and executable module-level statements are not supported in test entry files. ``` title: Math tests summary: Uses assertions in compiled tests. ``` import math from stdlib fn test_square() -> none: assert math.square(3) == 9 fn test_clamp() -> none: assert math.clamp(0 - 3, 0, 2) == 0, "lower bound" Run tests arx test arx test tests/test_math.x --list arx test -k square arx test -x arx test --keep-artifacts Use arx test --help for discovery and execution options, including selection, exclusion, and artifact retention. Project configuration Configure default discovery in .arxproject.toml : [tests] paths = ["tests", "integration"] exclude = ["tests/experimental_*.x"] file_pattern = "test_*.x" function_pattern = "test_*" CLI flags take precedence over project settings. Execution model For each selected test, the runner builds a synthetic module with a main function that calls exactly that test. IRx builds and links the executable. Assertion failures are returned through IRx's machine-readable assertion protocol and converted into test results. Use --keep-artifacts when inspecting generated wrappers or compiler output for a failing test. Arrow and Parquet CI coverage CI collects the complete package suites and compiled-language tests on Python 3.10–3.14. Native prerequisites are checked explicitly in Arx/IRx jobs so missing compilers or expected codecs cannot silently omit those integration paths. Installed-wheel smoke tests run in clean environments on Python 3.10 and 3.14, including the nullable Series native header and compiled kernel calls. A separate Linux job runs makim irx.test-sanitizers : registered Arrow and Parquet runtime artifacts are compiled with AddressSanitizer and UBSan. Its standalone harness exercises ownership/release, nullable scalar and Series outputs, invalid indices, overflow, and durable atomic Parquet round trips. Leak detection is enabled in CI. Third-party Arrow libraries are not rebuilt with instrumentation. Restricted local environments may run python scripts/test_native_sanitizers.py --no-leaks ; that is not evidence of a passing leak check. Live cloud-provider compatibility requires provisioned services and credentials and is not covered by these jobs. Local URI and unsupported transaction/error paths remain in the regular suites. No finite test suite proves every possible input or external-provider behavior.

text: Arrow and Parquet CI coverage CI collects the complete package suites and compiled-language tests on Python 3.10–3.14. Native prerequisites are checked explicitly in Arx/IRx jobs so missing compilers or expected codecs cannot silently omit those integration paths. Installed-wheel smoke tests run in clean environments on Python 3.10 and 3.14, including the nullable Series native header and compiled kernel calls. A separate Linux job runs makim irx.test-sanitizers : registered Arrow and Parquet runtime artifacts are compiled with AddressSanitizer and UBSan. Its standalone harness exercises ownership/release, nullable scalar and Series outputs, invalid indices, overflow, and durable atomic Parquet round trips. Leak detection is enabled in CI. Third-party Arrow libraries are not rebuilt with instrumentation. Restricted local environments may run python scripts/test_native_sanitizers.py --no-leaks ; that is not evidence of a passing leak check. Live cloud-provider compatibility requires provisioned services and credentials and is not covered by these jobs. Local URI and unsupported transaction/error paths remain in the regular suites. No finite test suite proves every possible input or external-provider behavior.
title: Compiled Tests · Arrow and Parquet CI coverage

text: Design: Python AST to ASTx lowering Status: staged implementation. Source extraction, Python-subset validation, signature reconciliation, and initial fail-closed ASTx lowering are implemented. IRx compilation, native bridging, caching, and dispatch are not. Goal Compile a restricted subset of pure, built-in Python through the existing Arx compiler stack. Users write ordinary Python and add @jit ; they do not embed Arx source strings or opt into another compiler backend. Pipeline status pure Python function -> source extraction implemented -> Python AST validation implemented -> signature resolution implemented -> ASTx lowering initial straight-line subset -> IRx/LLVM compilation not implemented -> native call bridge not implemented arxjit owns source handling, validation, the future Python-to-ASTx lowering, and the callable wrapper. ASTx owns the node model, while IRx owns semantic analysis, LLVM lowering, native runtime features, and artifact generation. The Arx source frontend is intentionally not in this path. Implemented frontend stages Decorator and signatures arxjit.core.jit returns a JitFunction that preserves the original function and records an optional explicit Signature plus the requested cache flag. JitFunction.__call__ currently calls the original Python function directly. The current scalar signature vocabulary is: i32 -> astx.Int32 i64 -> astx.Int64 f32 -> astx.Float32 f64 -> astx.Float64 bool_ -> astx.Boolean The astx_name metadata records the future lowering target; it does not mean that lowering already happens. Source extraction arxjit.source.extract_source() : unwraps decorated functions before inspection retrieves the defining file and exact function source removes decorators from the parsed function node preserves real-file line and column locations, including nested functions carries globals, closure names, and qualified-name context for validation translates retrieval and parse failures into structured diagnostics Source defined only through exec , lambdas, builtins, and other objects without retrievable function source are rejected. Validation arxjit.validation.validate() fails closed: an AST form must have an explicit accepted handler. The current proposed scalar subset includes: positional scalar arguments numeric and Boolean constants arithmetic, comparisons, Boolean expressions, and supported unary operators single-name assignments if / else and while without loop else for over the unshadowed builtin range with one to three positional args return , docstrings, and pass Unsupported forms produce one structured diagnostic per violation. Examples include imports, closures, methods, async code, exceptions, generators, collections, attributes, subscripting, comprehensions, break / continue , variadic/default arguments, and arbitrary calls. Implemented ASTx mapping The following straight-line mappings are implemented by arxjit.lowering : Python AST Proposed ASTx target ast.FunctionDef astx.FunctionDef and astx.FunctionPrototype argument astx.Argument inside astx.Arguments ast.Return astx.FunctionReturn ast.Name identifier/variable reference numeric or Boolean ast.Constant matching typed literal node ast.BinOp astx.BinaryOp ast.UnaryOp astx.UnaryOp ast.Compare comparison expression statement body astx.Block The lowerer builds a single-function astx.Module , uses the reconciled Signature , range-checks contextual literal widths, preserves source locations, mangles names reserved by IRx, and lowers expressions bottom-up. Boolean short-circuiting, chained comparisons, assignments, if , while , and for remain fail-closed because their Python evaluation semantics are not yet preserved. IRx remains the only owner of semantic analysis and feature lowering. Compilation and runtime work remaining After lowering, the design hands the module to irx.builder.Builder for translation and native artifact generation. ArxJIT still needs: assignment and control-flow ASTx lowering with Python semantics an in-process native callable bridge and scalar marshalling compilation and dispatch integration in JitFunction.__call__ a cache key covering source, signature, tool versions, and platform Signature inference is deferred; an explicit signature= remains the intended first compilation contract. Array, Tensor, and Apache Arrow-backed signatures are also deferred until scalar compilation and marshalling are stable.

text: ArxJIT ArxJIT is a developing Numba-style decorator path from a restricted subset of pure Python to ASTx, IRx, LLVM, and native callable code. Current behavior: decorated calls execute the original Python function. Initial Python-AST-to-ASTx lowering exists as a public, fail-closed stage, but the decorator does not invoke it and native compilation has not landed. Implemented foundations @jit and JitFunction explicit scalar signatures using i32 , i64 , f32 , f64 , and bool_ function-source extraction with corrected real-file source locations structured errors when source cannot be retrieved or parsed exhaustive validation and diagnostics for the proposed Python subset signature reconciliation from explicit signatures or reserved scalar annotations initial ASTx lowering for function shells, typed arguments and returns, scalar literals, parameter reads, arithmetic, supported unary operators, and single comparisons from arxjit import i64, jit @jit(signature=i64(i64, i64), cache=True) def add(left, right): return left + right assert add(20, 22) == 42 # Python fallback in the current implementation The current validator accepts scalar expressions, assignments, if / else , while , for over the unshadowed builtin range , and returns. Collections, closures, imports, methods, async code, generators, exceptions, attributes, and subscripting are rejected. The lowerer deliberately covers less than the validator. Assignments, Boolean short-circuit expressions, chained comparisons, and control flow still fail closed in lowering rather than producing an incomplete ASTx module. Deferred pipeline Python function -> source extraction implemented -> Python AST validation implemented -> signature resolution implemented -> ASTx lowering initial straight-line subset -> IRx native compilation not implemented -> Python-callable bridge not implemented Arrow-backed arrays and tensors are intentionally deferred until scalar compilation and runtime marshalling are stable. See the Python-to-ASTx design for the implemented frontend stages and remaining compilation work.

text: ArxPy ArxPy is the typed Python API for parsing, checking, compiling, and running Arx programs without invoking the CLI. Current status ArxPy now has a pre-stable end-to-end compiler facade. Implemented: Diagnostic and DiagnosticSeverity conversion helpers for IRx diagnostics and Arx parser failures ArxError as the public base exception ParseError , CompileError , and ExecutionError lightweight imports that do not initialize LLVM at module import time parse-from-string and parse-from-file entry points through Compiler semantic checking and structured diagnostic translation host LLVM IR, object, and executable artifacts captured execution with arguments, environment, working directory, and timeout runtime validation of public arguments and every collection item serialized repeated/concurrent operations while the frontend uses global input state Not yet stable or implemented: cancellation and asynchronous compilation cross-target selection and target discovery compiler test-discovery facade cache controls and a query/LSP protocol compatibility guarantees for the pre-1.0 facade Install pip install arxpy Usage from pathlib import Path from arxpy import ArtifactKind, Compiler compiler = Compiler() parsed = compiler.parse_file("program.x") checked = compiler.check(parsed) artifact = compiler.compile( checked, kind=ArtifactKind.EXECUTABLE, output=Path("build/program"), ) result = compiler.run(artifact, timeout=10) print(result.exit_code, result.stdout, result.stderr) Expected failures expose structured diagnostics: from arxpy import ArxError, Compiler try: Compiler().check(Compiler().parse_file("program.x")) except ArxError as error: for item in error.diagnostics: print(item.code, item.filename, item.line, item.column, item.message) In-memory native compilation requires an explicit output path. File compilation defaults beside the source. No implicit persistent temporary directory is created. Compiler calls are safe to repeat and are serialized across instances because the current lexer reads a process-wide source buffer. Execution never uses a shell; a non-zero program exit is returned in ExecutionResult rather than raised. Command arguments must be supplied as a non-string sequence of strings; scalar str and bytes values are rejected. Use the Arx CLI for compiler test discovery and other CLI-specific workflows. The roadmap tracks the remaining API stability work.

text: Contributing to ASTx ASTx lives in packages/astx within the ArxLang monorepo. Changes should keep the shared node model language-agnostic and should not embed Arx parser rules or IRx lowering behavior. Setup git clone https://github.com/arxlang/arx.git cd arx mamba env create --file conda/dev.yaml conda activate arx poetry install Change guidelines Reuse existing node families and naming conventions. Add source locations and parent relationships consistently. Keep runtime type checking and strict static typing green. Update __str__ , structured representation, and visualization behavior when node shape changes. Add focused tests under packages/astx/tests . Coordinate IRx and frontend changes when a new node is intended for immediate lowering or source-language use. Do not imply that adding an ASTx node automatically adds backend support. Checks makim astx.unittests makim astx.typecheck makim astx.lint makim astx.build Run makim all.ci when a change also touches Arx, IRx, or another package. Pull request titles use Conventional Commits because releases are generated by semantic-release and squash merge.

text: ASTx Code Styling and Conventions This document outlines the coding standards and conventions for the ASTx project. Following these guidelines ensures consistency, readability, and maintainability across the codebase. General Guidelines Type Safety: Always use the @typechecked decorator on all new ASTx classes to enforce runtime type checks. Additionally, do not reuse a variable for different types within the same context. Reference Existing Syntax: When implementing an ASTx class that corresponds to a Python syntax construct, refer to Python’s AST (e.g., using ast.dump(ast.parse("class MyClass:\n attr1: int = 1")) ) to validate that all necessary attributes and subnodes are correctly implemented. Avoid Excessive Nesting: Follow the "never nesting" approach to reduce code complexity. Review resources such as Never Nester – Why You Shouldn’t Nest Your Code and How and Why to Avoid Excessive Nesting . str Method Conventions Class Name: The __str__ method of an ASTx node should return the name of the class in CapitalizedCamelCase. Attributes Representation: If a node has one attribute (that is not another ASTx node), display it in square brackets immediately after the class name. Example: LiteralInt32[1] If a node has multiple non-ASTx attributes, list them with the attribute name(s) and value(s) separated by commas. Example: LiteralComplex32[real=1, imag=1] For boolean attributes, you may: Include the attribute name if its value is True (e.g., Class[abstract] ), omitting it if False . Alternatively, differentiate using distinct names (e.g., Class[static] vs. Class[non-static] ), as appropriate for the specific node. get_struct Method Conventions Naming Consistency: The key in the get_struct output should match the string returned by the node’s __str__ method. When the simplified flag is True , append #{id(self)} to the name to prevent grouping in ASCII representations. Sub-node Keys: Each sub-node in the structure should be represented with a key in lowercase using hyphen separators. Example: { "except": except_.get_struct(simplified), "finally-handler": finally_handler.get_struct(simplified) }

text: ASTx ASTx is the language-agnostic abstract syntax tree model shared by the ArxLang ecosystem. It lets frontends and compiler tools exchange typed Python objects without sharing a source grammar. Status: functional and evolving. ASTx can model constructs that IRx or a particular source language does not yet lower. Current capabilities common AST base classes, source locations, parents, and structured output identifiers, variables, literals, operators, statements, and blocks scalar, text, temporal, collection, generic, and finite-union types functions, modules, packages, imports, defaults, and templates conditionals, loops, comprehensions, generators, and context managers classes, structs, inheritance, member access, visibility, and mutability FFI pointers and opaque handles list, buffer-view, Tensor, DataFrame, and Series nodes YAML, JSON, Mermaid, PNG, and optional ASCII visualization Architecture boundary ASTx does not: lex or parse source code decide source-language syntax perform IRx semantic analysis provide native storage or depend on Apache Arrow guarantee backend lowering for every modeled node IRx consumes ASTx nodes and owns analysis, LLVM lowering, and the native Arrow C++ runtime. Source frontends such as Arx construct ASTx nodes. Small example import astx body = astx.Block() body.append(astx.FunctionReturn(astx.LiteralInt32(0))) main = astx.FunctionDef( prototype=astx.FunctionPrototype( name="main", args=astx.Arguments(), return_type=astx.Int32(), ), body=body, ) print(main.to_yaml()) License ASTx is licensed under Apache-2.0 as part of the ArxLang monorepo.

text: Installing ASTx Published package pip install astx ASTx supports Python 3.10 or newer. For console ASCII rendering through mermaid-ascii : pip install 'astx[console]' The all extra currently installs the same optional visualization dependency: pip install 'astx[all]' Without the optional console dependency, console rendering falls back to YAML. Source checkout ASTx is developed in the Arx monorepo: git clone https://github.com/arxlang/arx.git cd arx mamba env create --file conda/dev.yaml conda activate arx poetry install makim astx.unittests The root Poetry project installs packages/astx as an editable dependency.

text: Adding Nodes into Specific Contexts in ASTx Introduction In abstract syntax tree (AST) manipulations, context or scope management is crucial for correctly placing nodes within the tree. This tutorial will discuss two methods to add nodes into specific contexts or scopes using the ASTx library, which provides a comprehensive framework for constructing and manipulating ASTs. Setup Before you begin, make sure you have the ASTx library installed and imported in your Python environment: In [1] import astx In [2] # skip warnings import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") Example Setup We will explore two methods for adding nodes into specific contexts, 1) with append method into the parent object, and 2) with the parent attribute. Method 1: Using the parent Attribute One effective way to manage context is by directly adding new child nodes into the parent one. This method doesn't require the creation of the parent node first: In [3] # Initialize the ASTx module module = astx.Module() # Declare variables 'a', 'b', and 'c' with initial values decl_a = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="a", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(1)) decl_b = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="b", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(2)) decl_c = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="c", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(1)) # Reassign a new value to variable 'c' assign_c = astx.VariableAssignment(name="c", value=astx.LiteralInt32(3)) # Create ASTx Variable objects a = astx.Variable(name="a") b = astx.Variable(name="b") c = astx.Variable(name="c") # Create a literal integer lit_1 = astx.LiteralInt32(1) # Perform basic operations basic_op = lit_1 + b - a * c / a # Define the main function prototype main_proto = astx.FunctionPrototype( name="main", args=astx.Arguments(), return_type=astx.Int32() ) # Create a block of code and append variable declarations and operations main_block = astx.Block() main_block.append(decl_a) main_block.append(decl_b) main_block.append(decl_c) main_block.append(assign_c) main_block.append(astx.FunctionReturn(basic_op)) # Define the main function with its body main_fn = astx.FunctionDef(prototype=main_proto, body=main_block) # Append the main function to the module block module.block.append(main_fn) module Saved notebook output args body lhs lhs rhs rhs lhs lhs rhs rhs MODULE[main] FUNCTION-DEF[main] Arguments(0) BLOCK[entry-135197992911248] VariableDeclaration[a, Int32] Literal[Int32: temp_6]: 1 VariableDeclaration[b, Int32] Literal[Int32: temp_9]: 2 VariableDeclaration[c, Int32] Literal[Int32: temp_12]: 1 VariableAssignment[c] Literal[Int32: temp_14]: 3 RETURN BINARY[-] BINARY[+] Literal[Int32: temp_19]: 1 Variable[b] BINARY[/] BINARY[*] Variable[a] Variable[c] Using parent argument If you prefer to add a new node automatically into the parent node, you can use the parent argument, pointing it to the desired parent node: In [4] # Initialize the ASTx module module = astx.Module() main_block = astx.Block() # Define the main function prototype main_proto = astx.FunctionPrototype( name="main", args=astx.Arguments(), return_type=astx.Int32() ) # Define the main function with its body main_fn = astx.FunctionDef(prototype=main_proto, body=main_block, parent=module) # Declare variables 'a', 'b', and 'c' with initial values decl_a = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="a", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(1), parent=main_block) decl_b = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="b", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(2), parent=main_block) decl_c = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="c", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(1), parent=main_block) # Reassign a new value to variable 'c' assign_c = astx.VariableAssignment(name="c", value=astx.LiteralInt32(3), parent=main_block) # Create ASTx Variable objects a = astx.Variable(name="a") b = astx.Variable(name="b") c = astx.Variable(name="c") # Create a literal integer lit_1 = astx.LiteralInt32(1) # Perform basic operations basic_op = lit_1 + b - a * c / a astx.FunctionReturn(basic_op, parent=main_block) module Saved notebook output args body lhs lhs rhs rhs lhs lhs rhs rhs MODULE[main] FUNCTION-DEF[main] Arguments(0) BLOCK[entry-135197992912208] VariableDeclaration[a, Int32] Literal[Int32: temp_28]: 1 VariableDeclaration[b, Int32] Literal[Int32: temp_31]: 2 VariableDeclaration[c, Int32] Literal[Int32: temp_34]: 1 VariableAssignment[c] Literal[Int32: temp_36]: 3 RETURN BINARY[-] BINARY[+] Literal[Int32: temp_41]: 1 Variable[b] BINARY[/] BINARY[*] Variable[a] Variable[c] Conclusion In this tutorial, we explored two methods for adding nodes into specific contexts or scopes in ASTs using the ASTx library. By correctly managing the context of nodes, developers can ensure that the AST accurately represents the intended structure of the source code, which is essential for further analysis or transformations. Whether you choose to manually add the child node into the parent node or using the parent argument, ASTx provides the flexibility to suit various coding styles and requirements.

text: Fibonacci Sequence with ASTx Introduction The Fibonacci sequence is a series of numbers where each number is the sum of the two preceding ones, usually starting with 0 and 1. The sequence typically looks like this: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, and so on. It is a common example used to illustrate concepts in programming, including recursion and iterative loops. As mentioned by Fibonacci Sequence Wiki , the Fibonacci numbers may be defined by the recurrence relation: $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, and $F_n = F_{n−1} + F_{n−2}$ for n > 1. Under some older definitions, the value $F_0= 0$ is omitted, so that the sequence starts with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$, and the recurrence $F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$ is valid for n > 2. In this section, we'll demonstrate how to implement a Fibonacci sequence generator using ASTx. We'll focus on creating an AST for a function that computes Fibonacci numbers using an iterative approach. As a reference, let's use the following Python code: In [1] def fib(n: int): if n in {0, 1}: return n return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) In [2] # skip warnings import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") Steps to Implement Fibonacci with ASTx Define the Function Prototype : This includes the function name and parameters. Declare Variables : Variables needed for the iterative computation. Create the Loop : Implement the loop to compute the Fibonacci sequence. Return the Result : Return the computed Fibonacci number. Implementation Below is the Python code to create an AST for a Fibonacci function using ASTx. Note that the ASTx library and its components need to be defined as per your setup. text: Exploring For Loops in ASTx: A Detailed Guide Introduction Loops are a fundamental aspect of programming, offering a way to repeat a set of instructions under specific conditions. In this blog post, we'll delve into how ASTx, a versatile tool for manipulating abstract syntax trees (ASTs), handles two types of loops: the For Range Loop and the For Count Loop . Understanding these constructs in ASTx is crucial for anyone looking to automate or analyze code patterns efficiently. Setting Up Before we dive into the specifics of loop creation in ASTx, let's start by setting up our environment. This step is as simple as importing the ASTx library: In [1] import astx In [2] import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") With ASTx imported, we're now ready to explore the different types of loops it supports. For Range Loop The For Range Loop in ASTx allows you to specify the starting point, end condition, and iteration step. This loop is especially useful for scenarios where you need to iterate over a range of values. In [3] # Declare a loop variable decl_a = astx.InlineVariableDeclaration( "a", type_=astx.Int32(), ) # Create a block for loop body body_for = astx.Block() body_for.append( astx.VariableAssignment( name="x", value=astx.Variable("a") + astx.LiteralInt32(1) ) ) # Define a For Range Expression from 0 to 10 with step 1 for_1000 = astx.ForRangeLoopExpr( start=astx.LiteralInt32(0), end=astx.LiteralInt32(10), step=astx.LiteralInt32(1), variable=decl_a, body=body_for ) for_1000 Saved notebook output var start end step lhs rhs FOR-RANGE-LOOP-EXPR InlineVariableDeclaration[a, Int32] UNDEFINED Literal[Int32: temp_10]: 0 Literal[Int32: temp_12]: 10 Literal[Int32: temp_14]: 1 BLOCK[entry-133155269961168] VariableAssignment[x] BINARY[+] Variable[a] Literal[Int32: temp_7]: 1 In this example, we declare an inline variable a of type Int32 . text: Get Started Introduction The ASTx library is an agnostic framework for constructing and representing Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs). Its primary objective is to provide a versatile and language-independent structure for ASTs, with the flexibility to be utilized across various programming languages and parsing tools. ASTx doesn't aim to be a lexer or a parser, although it could be used by any programming language or parser in order to provide a high level representation of the AST. Many kinds of nodes (classes) are currently supported. Below is a list with just some examples: Statements: FunctionDef Function Prototype FunctionReturn ForRangeLoop VarDecl Operators: BinaryOp UnaryOp Data types: Boolean Literal Variable The ASTx project is still under development, so new classes may be added to the ones above at any time. Below are installation instructions and an example, so you can have an overview of how you can leverage the ASTx library for your needs. Installation The first step is to install ASTx. You can do it simply by running the command below in your terminal: $ pip install astx If you need more information on installation, you can get it in the ASTx installation page . After that, you can just open a Jupyter Notebook instance and start writing your first AST. Example: an AST of a series of mathematical operations Here we will present a quick example of an AST of the expression basic_op = lit_1 + b - a * c / a + (b - a / a) , in which $~~~~$ lit_1 is a defined integer, and $~~~~$ a , b , and c are variables. The first thing to do is, in your Jupyter Notebook instance, import display , which will allow you to have a basic visualization of the AST, and the astx library itself. In [1] # import display for AST visualization from IPython.display import display from astx.viz import visualize_ascii import astx In [2] # skip warnings import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") Then we create an instance of the Module class, and this instance will be the first node of the tree, or the root node. After that, we declare the variables and literal that will be part of the basic operation that we will parse into an AST. In [3] # Create module module = astx.Module() # Declare variables decl_a = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="a", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(1)) decl_b = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="b", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(2)) decl_c = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="c", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(4)) a = astx.Variable(name="a") b = astx.Variable(name="b") c = astx.Variable(name="c") # Declare literal lit_1 = astx.LiteralInt32(1) # State the expression basic_op = lit_1 + b - a * c / a + (b - a / a) After the basic expression is stated, we create an instance of the FunctionDef class. As mentioned in the API documentation, each instance of the FunctionDef class must have a prototype and a body, so we'll create those first. The body is made of a block that is created and the variables, as well as the basic operation, are appended to it afterwards. In [4] # Create FunctionPrototype main_proto = astx.FunctionPrototype( name="main", args=astx.Arguments(), return_type=astx.Int32() ) # Create FunctionReturn main_block = astx.Block() main_block.append(decl_a) main_block.append(decl_b) main_block.append(decl_c) main_block.append(astx.FunctionReturn(basic_op)) # Create Function main_fn = astx.FunctionDef(prototype=main_proto, body=main_block) # Append function to module module.block.append(main_fn) After this, the module is complete. title: Get Started

text: Introduction The ASTx library is an agnostic framework for constructing and representing Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs). Its primary objective is to provide a versatile and language-independent structure for ASTs, with the flexibility to be utilized across various programming languages and parsing tools. ASTx doesn't aim to be a lexer or a parser, although it could be used by any programming language or parser in order to provide a high level representation of the AST. Many kinds of nodes (classes) are currently supported. Below is a list with just some examples: Statements: FunctionDef Function Prototype FunctionReturn ForRangeLoop VarDecl Operators: BinaryOp UnaryOp Data types: Boolean Literal Variable The ASTx project is still under development, so new classes may be added to the ones above at any time. Below are installation instructions and an example, so you can have an overview of how you can leverage the ASTx library for your needs.
title: Get Started · Introduction

text: Installation The first step is to install ASTx. You can do it simply by running the command below in your terminal: $ pip install astx If you need more information on installation, you can get it in the ASTx installation page . After that, you can just open a Jupyter Notebook instance and start writing your first AST.
title: Get Started · Installation

text: Example: an AST of a series of mathematical operations Here we will present a quick example of an AST of the expression basic_op = lit_1 + b - a * c / a + (b - a / a) , in which $~~~~$ lit_1 is a defined integer, and $~~~~$ a , b , and c are variables. The first thing to do is, in your Jupyter Notebook instance, import display , which will allow you to have a basic visualization of the AST, and the astx library itself. In [1] # import display for AST visualization from IPython.display import display from astx.viz import visualize_ascii import astx In [2] # skip warnings import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") Then we create an instance of the Module class, and this instance will be the first node of the tree, or the root node. After that, we declare the variables and literal that will be part of the basic operation that we will parse into an AST. In [3] # Create module module = astx.Module() # Declare variables decl_a = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="a", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(1)) decl_b = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="b", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(2)) decl_c = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="c", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(4)) a = astx.Variable(name="a") b = astx.Variable(name="b") c = astx.Variable(name="c") # Declare literal lit_1 = astx.LiteralInt32(1) # State the expression basic_op = lit_1 + b - a * c / a + (b - a / a) After the basic expression is stated, we create an instance of the FunctionDef class. As mentioned in the API documentation, each instance of the FunctionDef class must have a prototype and a body, so we'll create those first. The body is made of a block that is created and the variables, as well as the basic operation, are appended to it afterwards. In [4] # Create FunctionPrototype main_proto = astx.FunctionPrototype( name="main", args=astx.Arguments(), return_type=astx.Int32() ) # Create FunctionReturn main_block = astx.Block() main_block.append(decl_a) main_block.append(decl_b) main_block.append(decl_c) main_block.append(astx.FunctionReturn(basic_op)) # Create Function main_fn = astx.FunctionDef(prototype=main_proto, body=main_block) # Append function to module module.block.append(main_fn) After this, the module is complete. We can get its AST structure as a dictionary, as well as a PNG representation. text: Literals in ASTx Introduction Literals are fixed values embedded directly in source code, representing specific values. They are the raw data given in variables or constants and are not variables themselves but the data assigned to them. Common types of literals found in many programming languages include: Integer Literals : Represent whole numbers without any fractional component, e.g., 42 , -1 , 0 . Floating-Point Literals : Represent real numbers with fractional parts, e.g., 3.14 , -0.01 . String Literals : Enclose sequences of characters, typically in quotes, e.g., "hello" , 'world' . Boolean Literals : Represent truth values, usually denoted by true and false . Null/None Literals : Represent the absence of a value or a null reference, e.g., null in Java, None in Python. Character Literals : Represent single characters, e.g., 'a' , 'Z' . Array or List Literals : Define arrays or lists directly, e.g., [1, 2, 3] in Python. Object Literals : Used in languages like JavaScript to define objects directly, e.g., {name: "Alice", age: 25} . Currently, ASTx just support integer literals (8, 16, 32, and 64 bits) and boolean literals, but the support for new ones should be done soon. Example Let's check a very some examples of the usage of literals with ASTx : In [1] import astx In [2] # skip warnings import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") In [3] astx.LiteralInt8(value=1) Saved notebook output <IPython.core.display.Image object> In [4] astx.LiteralInt16(value=1) Saved notebook output <IPython.core.display.Image object> In [5] astx.LiteralInt32(value=1) Saved notebook output <IPython.core.display.Image object> In [6] astx.LiteralInt64(value=1) Saved notebook output <IPython.core.display.Image object> In [7] astx.LiteralBoolean(value=True) Saved notebook output <IPython.core.display.Image object> Now, let's check how a math operation over literals would look like: In [8] lit_1_a = astx.LiteralInt32(value=1) lit_1_b = astx.LiteralInt32(value=1) lit_2 = astx.LiteralInt32(value=2) (lit_1_a + lit_1_b + lit_2) Saved notebook output <IPython.core.display.Image object> Conclusion Literals are features really fundamental in any programming language. Currently, ASTx supports supports Integers (8, 16, 32, and 64 bits) and Boolean, and much more should be implemented soon!

text: Understanding Variables in ASTx: A Comprehensive Guide Introduction In the world of programming, the concept of variables is fundamental, acting as the cornerstone for writing effective and efficient code. However, the way variables are declared and used can vary significantly across different programming languages. This variability poses a challenge for tools that need to operate across these languages, such as ASTx. ASTx, an advanced tool for manipulating abstract syntax trees (ASTs), addresses this challenge by offering a generic approach to handling variables. This blog post delves into the nuances of working with variables in ASTx, providing insights into both declaration and usage, with a focus on simplicity and generality. Setting Up the Environment To get started with variables in ASTx, you need to set up your Python environment appropriately. This setup involves importing necessary modules and ensuring that your environment is primed for the tasks ahead. Here's how you can set it up: First, ensure you have astx installed: $ pip install astx Now, you can import the libraries and modules necessary for this tutorial: In [1] from __future__ import annotations import copy from typing import Any from IPython.display import display import astx In [2] # skip warnings import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") This code block sets the stage for our exploration into ASTx's variable handling. We're importing essential modules like copy for deep copying objects, typing for type annotations, and IPython.display for displaying outputs in an interactive Python environment. Most importantly, we import astx , the library central to our discussion. Creating Variables and Performing Simple Math Now, let's dive into the practical aspects of variable declaration and usage in ASTx, particularly how these variables can be used in basic mathematical operations. In [3] # Initialize the ASTx module module = astx.Module() # Declare variables 'a', 'b', and 'c' with initial values decl_a = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="a", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(1)) decl_b = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="b", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(2)) decl_c = astx.VariableDeclaration(name="c", type_=astx.Int32(), value=astx.LiteralInt32(4)) # Reassign a new value to variable 'c' assign_c = astx.VariableAssignment(name="c", value=astx.LiteralInt32(3)) # Create ASTx Variable objects a = astx.Variable(name="a") b = astx.Variable(name="b") c = astx.Variable(name="c") # Create a literal integer lit_1 = astx.LiteralInt32(1) # Perform basic operations basic_op = lit_1 + b - a * c / a # Define the main function prototype main_proto = astx.FunctionPrototype( name="main", args=astx.Arguments(), return_type=astx.Int32() ) # Create a block of code and append variable declarations and operations main_block = astx.Block() main_block.append(decl_a) main_block.append(decl_b) main_block.append(decl_c) main_block.append(assign_c) main_block.append(astx.FunctionReturn(basic_op)) # Define the main function with its body main_fn = astx.FunctionDef(prototype=main_proto, body=main_block) # Append the main function to the module block module.block.append(main_fn) module Saved notebook output <IPython.core.display.Image object> In this code snippet, we start by initializing an ASTx module. We then declare three variables ( a , b , and c ) with initial integer values using VarDecl . Interestingly, we demonstrate how to reassign a new value to an existing variable ( c in this case). The Variable class in ASTx is used to create variable objects that can be manipulated further. Next, we create a simple mathematical operation involving these variables, showcasing how ASTx can elegantly handle arithmetic expressions. The code concludes with the creation of a main function prototype, a block of code containing our declarations and operations, and the definition of the main function itself. Conclusion This exploration into the world of variables within ASTx reveals the power and flexibility of this tool. By abstracting the intricacies of variable handling across different programming languages, ASTx provides a unified and streamlined approach. Whether you are a seasoned developer or just starting, understanding how to effectively declare and manipulate variables in ASTx is a valuable skill in your programming toolkit.

Builtin and single-inheritance user exception classes use ordinary nominal identities; causes and dynamic bare re-raise are supported. Checked numeric, assertion, bounds, file, and Arrow/CSV/Parquet failures are catchable. Finalizers and owned-resource cleanup run before propagation; implicit cleanup preserves a primary failure and records secondary failures. try , except , finally , and raise are reserved keywords. ASTx now models cause/else clauses and qualified handler references; ThrowStmt.get_struct() names its children. Empty handler type lists are not catch-all handlers. Generated functions and runtime callbacks use a context/status/result-slot ABI; rebuild all native producers and consumers together. Ordinary external C signatures remain unchanged. Uncaught failures use structured exception reports; ArxPy exposes them as execution-result data, not Python exceptions. Protected regions spanning generator suspension, Python traceback mutation, exception groups, asynchronous exceptions, and ArxJIT exception lowering remain unsupported. See the support boundary . Checked numeric promotion (breaking) Numeric promotion and implicit conversions are now lossless across the whole source domain. Mixed signed/unsigned comparisons no longer reinterpret negatives; combinations without a common domain require an explicit cast. Integer arithmetic and numeric casts now fail on out-of-range results in all builds. Source literals retain context and signed minima until type checking. math.square preserves its selected type and fails on overflow; widen its input or explicitly select a wider specialization before computing. Use wrapping_add , wrapping_sub , wrapping_mul , and wrapping_cast only where modulo arithmetic is intended. Ordinary narrowing no longer truncates silently. Nonidentity Series/tensor casts are explicitly unsupported. ArxJIT lowering shares IRx numeric promotion; integer source literals use i32-then-i64 inference and must remain exact in floating contexts. Python @jit fallback and the reserved int annotation (i64) are unchanged. ASTx contextual numeric nodes are LiteralInteger and LiteralFloat , in astx.literals . LiteralFloat accepts exact decimal text or Decimal , not Python float . These replace SourceInteger / SourceFloat without aliases. IRx preserves literal payloads and resolves types and rounded values only in semantic metadata, avoiding decimal-to-f32/f16 double rounding. Direct ASTx/IRx clients must analyze numeric nodes before lowering. Arithmetic and conversion plans, including union storage, are authoritative sidecars. See the numeric safety contract . Integer helper safety and templates range now terminates without wrapping when a step crosses an i32 endpoint; it still returns an eagerly allocated list[i32] . stdlib.math scalar helpers now use a shared signed-integer template bound for i8 , i16 , i32 , and i64 , preserving the selected result type. stdlib.math.abs on the selected type's minimum now fails checked arithmetic; clamp with reversed bounds raises AssertionError ; abs overflow raises OverflowError . These failures can be handled by exception statements. Migration notes Math helpers no longer convert every call to i32 . Inferred arguments must have the same concrete signed type; use casts or explicit specialization, such as math.min<i64>(small, wide) , when mixing widths. Floating-point, unsigned, Boolean, and nullable specializations remain unsupported. CSV and Parquet operations live in stdlib.csv and stdlib.parquet ; stdlib.arrow retains shared schemas, batches, and IPC. Use CSVStream and ParquetStream for explicit sessions instead of the removed CSV and Parquet class names. No compatibility aliases are provided. text: Python-inspired exceptions (breaking) raise , ordered except handlers, else , and finally now propagate across generated calls. Builtin and single-inheritance user exception classes use ordinary nominal identities; causes and dynamic bare re-raise are supported. Checked numeric, assertion, bounds, file, and Arrow/CSV/Parquet failures are catchable. Finalizers and owned-resource cleanup run before propagation; implicit cleanup preserves a primary failure and records secondary failures. try , except , finally , and raise are reserved keywords. ASTx now models cause/else clauses and qualified handler references; ThrowStmt.get_struct() names its children. Empty handler type lists are not catch-all handlers. Generated functions and runtime callbacks use a context/status/result-slot ABI; rebuild all native producers and consumers together. Ordinary external C signatures remain unchanged. Uncaught failures use structured exception reports; ArxPy exposes them as execution-result data, not Python exceptions. Protected regions spanning generator suspension, Python traceback mutation, exception groups, asynchronous exceptions, and ArxJIT exception lowering remain unsupported. See the support boundary .
title: Release Notes · Python-inspired exceptions (breaking)

text: Checked numeric promotion (breaking) Numeric promotion and implicit conversions are now lossless across the whole source domain. Mixed signed/unsigned comparisons no longer reinterpret negatives; combinations without a common domain require an explicit cast. Integer arithmetic and numeric casts now fail on out-of-range results in all builds. Source literals retain context and signed minima until type checking. math.square preserves its selected type and fails on overflow; widen its input or explicitly select a wider specialization before computing. Use wrapping_add , wrapping_sub , wrapping_mul , and wrapping_cast only where modulo arithmetic is intended. Ordinary narrowing no longer truncates silently. Nonidentity Series/tensor casts are explicitly unsupported. ArxJIT lowering shares IRx numeric promotion; integer source literals use i32-then-i64 inference and must remain exact in floating contexts. Python @jit fallback and the reserved int annotation (i64) are unchanged. ASTx contextual numeric nodes are LiteralInteger and LiteralFloat , in astx.literals . LiteralFloat accepts exact decimal text or Decimal , not Python float . These replace SourceInteger / SourceFloat without aliases. IRx preserves literal payloads and resolves types and rounded values only in semantic metadata, avoiding decimal-to-f32/f16 double rounding. Direct ASTx/IRx clients must analyze numeric nodes before lowering. Arithmetic and conversion plans, including union storage, are authoritative sidecars. See the numeric safety contract .
title: Release Notes · Checked numeric promotion (breaking)

text: Integer helper safety and templates range now terminates without wrapping when a step crosses an i32 endpoint; it still returns an eagerly allocated list[i32] . stdlib.math scalar helpers now use a shared signed-integer template bound for i8 , i16 , i32 , and i64 , preserving the selected result type. stdlib.math.abs on the selected type's minimum now fails checked arithmetic; clamp with reversed bounds raises AssertionError ; abs overflow raises OverflowError . These failures can be handled by exception statements.
title: Release Notes · Integer helper safety and templates

text: Migration notes Math helpers no longer convert every call to i32 . Inferred arguments must have the same concrete signed type; use casts or explicit specialization, such as math.min<i64>(small, wide) , when mixing widths. Floating-point, unsigned, Boolean, and nullable specializations remain unsupported. CSV and Parquet operations live in stdlib.csv and stdlib.parquet ; stdlib.arrow retains shared schemas, batches, and IPC. Use CSVStream and ParquetStream for explicit sessions instead of the removed CSV and Parquet class names. No compatibility aliases are provided. Module-level read_csv / write_csv and read_parquet / write_parquet remain the eager path.
